I see some complaints about the enemy leveling in the game so I'd like to take a chance to at least let players know what they are getting into specifically before had and how it works with a quick rundown of how it works. When you first enter an area in remnant, the average level of your gear (known as gear score) is taken and that is essentially the level of the enemies that will spawn in that area until you regenerate that area by restarting the campaign. So, i enter a floor of a dungeon at level 4, i clear it and enter the boss room at 4 as well. If I'm unprepared for that boss and getting absolutely shafted, its an option to backtrack to the previous area, which remains level 4, raise my gear level to 5, and then go beat the boss, which would still be at level 4. Going to the area after the boss would have it set to 5 in this scenario. It allows you the chance to go against bosses at a similar strength level to what the devs intended originally without allowing for vast levels of variation. If you prefer the challenge, you can go at the boss all you want and work on beating it at the intended level. On my first playthrough, i only had to go back and farm a level for around 2 of the bosses. 

Hope someone will take a second to read this and at least have an idea of how it works. People just assume its autoscaling in every area without the full clearing of the campaign but that is not the case.

Remnant: From the Ashes is a souls-like third person RPG shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world. 

[h1] The strenghts [/h1] 

[list]
    [*][b]Short but interesting story: [/b]
While the story only plays a minor part in this game, it still keeps the player engaged. Expect around 10-15 hours on your first playthrough, later on when geared you can finish the story in around 4 hours. The whole game is built around your character. You start in your hideout where merchants are supplying you. From there, you decide what you want to do and where you want to go. The main focus definitely lies in the action packed gameplay.

    [*][b]Souls-like: [/b]
Fight through hordes of enemies in order to get to one of the 25 Dungeon Bosses or 12 World Bosses. Even normal enemies can kill you if you don't pay attention. Make use of their weakpoints. They did a great job making each boss unique and challenging without actually overtuning them. Expect to die... a lot, yet each defeated boss feels super rewarding afterwards. The best part is, unlike most of the other souls-like games, you don't lose anything upon death.

    [*][b]Unique Loot: [/b]
The game offers a plethora of weapons, armors, necklaces and rings, each with it's own effect and purpose. In total you can chose between 12 Handguns, 17 Long guns and 20 Melee Weapons. In addition to that, there are 18 different armor sets, 36 necklaces and 74 rings that you can chose from in order to customize your loadout. All items are either dropped by bosses, or hidden in the world/dungeons

    [*][b]Play what you want, how you want it: [/b]
As mentioned above there is a huge variety of items you can use for every type of encounter. You also have 40 weapon modifications (active skills) most of which you can freely equip onto your weapons. Leveling only affects your passive abilities. Every time you level up you can put a point into one of the 50 passive traits (each is capped at lvl 20, so 1000 is max level). There are dozens of viable endgame builds, play as a summoner, a caster, a stealthy Sniper, nuke the shit out of bosses or go a full tank/sustain build, the possibilities are endless. 

    [*][b]Enourmous replayability: [/b]
Every area is randomly generated, that means that no playthrough is the same. You get other dungeons, other bosses and also different loot. This encourages replaying the campaign in order to collect other items and face different enemies. The other gamemodes add to that:

- Adventure Mode:
compact, arcade-like campaign mode. You chose a world and difficulty and the game randomly generates a map with different loot, dungeons and bosses each time. Great to see new bosses, get the alternative kill on the world bosses or especially to find new items.

- Survival Mode:
Start from scratch in this mode. You are given 1000€, buy some basic items and venture into the wild. Books you find in the world give random traits and chests contain further gear. Basically you run through one of the different maps and a boss is waiting at the end. Then you return to the startpoint and can further gear up. It's a great mode in order to play with different armors, weapons and mods. The goal is to kill as many bosses as possible. But beware, the enemies grow stronger over time so don't explore too much. If you die, the run is over and you are back at the starting point in underwear. Account wide items (ring/necklace) are unlocked once you reach different perks (for example a nice sword after 10 consecutive boss kills)

- Hardcore Mode
It's basically the same campaign with a permadeath feature. If you die only once you have to start over. Also here you can unlock up to 9 account wide items that are unlocked after killing world bosses in hardcore mode

    [*][b]Everything can be played COOP: [/b]
Probably the best part about this game is that all content can be played in coop with up to 2 friends. After finishing the short tutorial you can basically directly invite your friends or join a friends game. As mentioned at the beginning, your character is the main focus, so every item you unlock is granted to your character, regardless if you are playing your campaign, or joining a friends lobby. And if noone is available or you are tired of playing solo, simply join a random lobby online.

    [*][b] Difficulty [/b]
The game offers 4 different difficulties, but since the story only plays a minor part they balanced it pretty well that even the lowest difficulty can be quite tough, especially in the beginning. This makes each successful boss kill super rewarding and higher difficulties pose a real challenge even for veteran players.

    [*][b] Music [/b]
The addition of great music makes slaying world bosses a truly epic adventure.

    [*][b] Great for occasional play: [/b]
While the game has enough to offer to hardcore play it for weeks, it is also great for occasional game sessions. Adventure mode runs take around 30-60 mins and survival mode runs also keep things fresh even after unlocking everything.
[/list]

[h1] The weaknesses [/h1]

[list]
    [*][b]Collecting can be grindy [/b]
Remnants biggest strenght in creating endless replayablity through randomly generating everything is also it's biggest flaw if you are looking for specific items, or in general trying to collect every item. You never know what your adventure mode or campaign has to offer unless you use a 3rd party programm (world analyzer) and keep re-rolling until you get your drop. Some items have insane rng requirements where several events have to be rolled in the same adventure in order to obtain them (ring of the unclean, blessed necklace)

    [*][b]Hidden stuff [/b]
Some items are almost impossible to get unless you do some research in the wiki. While i really like that exploring gets rewarded, sometimes things are so well hidden that you won't find it without external help (Potency trait/Ring of the Unclean, Letos armor)

    [*][b]No loadouts [/b]
For a game that offers endless possibilities of combining your gear it is beyond me that there is no option to save several loadouts for fast switching builds depending on the encounter. The Endgame pretty much consists of testing new builds or adapting to bosses you are facing. At some point it gets tedious scrolling down the 70 rings to find the one you need for your build.

    [*][b] Bugs [/b]
Most of these are minor annoyances, or barely noticeable. But sometimes it affects traits or items or even whole parts of the map. The game won't receive any content updates but the developers are still rolling out bugfixes, so most of the stuff will be eventually fixed.

    [*][b] Voiceacting [/b]
Glad the story isnt the main focus. The VA serves it's purpose, but it's far from good. 
[/list]

[h1] Final thoughts [/h1]

Remnant: From the ashes is definitly a great game. The intriguing part is that you are able to play it coop which makes for great evenings with friends. Theorycrafting after failed boss encounters and the hype after beating them for the first time is definitly a big plus. Grab both DLCs as they add tons of new equipent and the survival mode is a great challenge, also for veterans. I'll leave you with some useful Links so you can ask for help if you ever need it. [h2]Remnant: From the Ashes Review[/h2]

Less punishing souls-like game with a gorgeously detailed environment. Join this third-person survival action shooter set in a post-apocalyptic world full of monstrous creatures. Face the horde of bloodthirsty enemies solo, or with up to two other friends. The game undoubtedly is a love child of varied games. You will see the resemblance of Dark Souls during boss rushes, Fallout from the post-apocalyptic environment, Sea of Thieves’ in the graphics, and SCP foundation in the horror fiction. Alongside challenging gameplay, you can also upgrade your gear and rerun the worlds with a randomly generated campaign.

[h1]Gameplay:[/h1]
The scene starts with your character washed up on an island with nothing but clothes and a rusty sword. The story commences with a slow build-up, but when you reach Ward 13(bunker) and start the reactor, the game takes an exciting start. There are few NPCs at the spawn point, so it’s pretty easy to remember the map segments. The game solely wants you to engage in the action and face the monsters. With all the gear modifications and three different class selections, gameplay becomes quite challenging and do-able at the same time, which makes the game super fun and interesting. In order to survive the wrath of this madness, you need to get a hold of the dodge mechanism. If you are worried about the game lacking in the variation of bosses, then just chill and enter the madness of the monstrous world. You don’t need to worry about the length of the playthrough, as it’s quite promising.

[h1]Graphics:[/h1]
This definitely meets the quality of new-gen games with its brilliant and eye-pleasing graphics. The detailing on the map is spectacular. Every boss is uniquely designed and impressively balances with the environment’s color palette. Many of the games have bosses that look lifeless, but the developers here managed to depict a life form that might actually exist. Even with the rich detailing, the GPU consumption is not critically high. You can easily play the game in genuine settings without experiencing any lag. You will surely encounter some areas where you will be obliged to take a screenshot because of the colorful and eye-popping scenery.

[h1]Why the campaign is different from other games:[/h1]
The game has a unique way of keeping you engaged in the game for a long time by randomizing the campaign. Playthroughs are entirely different for everyone. The bosses are mainly classified within two divisions: dungeon boss and world boss. Dungeon bosses or mini-bosses are an upgraded version of regular enemies. On the other hand, defeating world bosses will move the plot forward. all world bosses in your playthrough, but that's why the game grants you the ability to reroll the campaign for a possibility of facing new bosses at the cost of increasing the world difficulty. Another way is to join multiplayer worlds of other players to seek out new bosses that might not have appeared in your world.. Adventure mode brings a new layer of exploration, by allowing players to re-roll the following biomes: Ruined Earth, Rhom, and Yaesha without having to play the whole campaign again.

[h1]Main Pros and Cons:[/h1]

[b]Pros-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Great visuals
    [*]Fun gameplay
    [*]Variation in playthrough 
    [*]Astonishing Bosses
    [*]A less punishing Dark Souls-like game
    [*]Exciting to play with friends
    [*]No pay-to-win
[/list]

[b]Cons-[/b]
[list]
    [*]Can be hard and boring to play alone
    [*]Encountering  all bosses might consume lot of time and tries
    [*]Lot of crash reports
    [*]Most of the bosses feel like a survival wave instead of one on one battle
[/list]

[h1]Tips to new players:[/h1]
If you are unaware of Dark Souls-like games, then it’s highly recommended to play with friends, as you might die in just 2 hits. Avoid selling scraps in the beginning, as they will be required for gear upgrades later in the game. Even though the classes are somewhat similar, choosing ex-Cultist might give you a bit of a head-start. Easter egg for all the lovely readers, when you begin your first mission and claim the keycard, a particular bookshelf might seem like it’s hiding something. 😉

[h1] Miscellaneous Information:[/h1]
[b]Info about DLCs-[/b]
Both the DLCs are worth it if you are looking to increase playtime by a lot. It offers new zones, new bosses, new weapon mods, some hidden puzzles/dungeons, and much more. Highly recommended during sales.

[h1]Honest Rating:[/h1]
The game fulfills your desire of playing a beautiful dungeon crawler that isn't as constantly difficult as Dark Souls. It’s a fun challenge that you can do alone or with friends and have a great time. Even though it’s a mix of a lot of games, it still feels unique and memorable.

Rating: 9/10
Some bosses haunt me in dreams.

[h1]A One-of-a-Kind Gem in Need of a Little More Polish[/h1]

If nothing else, Remnant: From the Ashes is undoubtedly something you've never seen before: no one would correct you if you named it a souls-like, a third-person shooter, or even a roguelite or RPG to some extent, as elements of all are present to differing capacity. Naturally, there can be issues in treading new ground: these borrowed aspects don't always work, and I think, for me, most of them didn't, at least not to the potential they could have, but supporting the entire experience is a combat model that is so exceptional in every respect, that it's hard to envision a world where Remnant could even come close to failing.

[h3]Procedural Generation and Exploration[/h3]

Remnant's use of procedural generation is a novel idea: each player's campaign will follow the same structure, but the precise layout of the world can see some considerable variation, along with the scenarios and bosses that inhabit it. Level design and exploration, however, are miserable as a result: in the name of making the experience malleable, to feel 'different' every time, the building blocks that make up the playable space are tragically basic and lifeless: there's almost nothing of interest to see or find, no hidden, enticing side routes, no intention behind enemy placement and, although they're built this way to aid in creating unique campaigns, they're [i]so[/i] simple that they have the opposite effect; the procedural generation degrades Remnant to a corridor simulator with a semi-random boss at the end of each one.

Furthermore, as almost everything is up to RNG, there's very little in the way of guaranteed loot and your build, for the most part, comes down to simply using what you find, regardless of whether or not you want to; there's every chance that you'll never find a weapon that suits you, or create a build that fits your desired playstyle. With Adventure Mode, separate from your campaign progress, you can freely make new instances of worlds already conquered to see new scenarios and the loot they offer; however, there's no guarantee you'll roll anything different from the first time you explored that world, there's often an unpleasant grind involved should you be looking for a particular item, and, the real issue, as I've already discussed, the procedural generation simply isn't robust enough to allow these replays to feel unique, interesting, or worth the time invested.

Finally, many optional questlines aren't entirely present. For example, early on, there's a chance you can meet with Mud Tooth, an elderly fellow living in a downed helicopter who'll offer you a pocket watch after listening to his stories, all the while informing you that he had intended to pass it along to his son Brabus one day. A less obvious quest there never was; however, it's all too common for a world seed to, despite including Mud Tooth, never house the boss encounter against Brabus, in which you can give him the watch to de-escalate the situation, skipping the fight while earning unique rewards. Worse yet, your seed could include Brabus but have the battle occur [i]before[/i] meeting his father, resulting in obtaining the watch after having already fought and killed the intended recipient. Adventure mode allows you to eventually roll the remainder of your incomplete quests should you wish, although this approach suffers all the same pitfalls outlined earlier.

[h3]Combat[/h3]

Very damning so far, I know, but in truth, Remnant's phenomenal combat mitigates many of these issues, at least enough for them to be tolerable: they're still there and very much noticeable; however, it's easy to forget how bland and lifeless the playable space is when you're so eager to get to the next fight, and failing to find the particular weapon you're looking for stings considerably less when every gun shoots like a dream.

So why is this combat model as brilliant as it is? I could go on and on about the superb sound design, the hefty, powerful weapons or the precise and dextrous controls, though as good as they are, it's the finer details that really shine: it's the thoughtfully designed enemy variants that compliment each other impeccably, keeping every encounter intense, it's the perfectly tuned stagger in each bullet that allows even the precision weapons to feel viable controlling the crowds at close range, it's the elegant consumable economy that offers the satisfaction of thoughtful preparation, yet keeps itself slim, not overwhelming with dozens of highly specific and hardly usable concoctions; every facet of battle feels meticulously scrutinised and subsequently optimised.

All except one, however. Remnant's boss battles are not at all consistent: on the one hand, you have original, multi-phase fights that deliver a fair and rewarding challenge; on the other, you have essentially reskinned elite enemies with two attacks that rely on sending a continuous, overwhelming stream of adds to mask the inadequacy of the boss itself, all the while making the encounter a nightmare for a solo player. Once again, we have another victim of the procedural generation; there are far more bosses than you'll ever see in one playthrough, and, unfortunately, there's an obvious case of quantity over quality here.

[h3]Character Progression[/h3]

I love what Gunfire Games went for here: there's a trait system offering quality-of-life improvements and increases to core stats after allocating points earned as you kill enemies and complete quests. Fairly standard so far, but not all of these traits are available to a new character: some will unlock after specific boss encounters, but more interesting are the ones that unlock based on the way you play or how your character has progressed; the 'climber' trait, for example, becomes available after vaulting obstacles fifty times and, as you might expect, increases your vault speed with each point allocated into it.

It's a great system on paper, moulding your character based on their experiences and one of the better aspects of the procedural generation; however, trait points feel slow to accumulate, and each one allocated provides little to no value. Take that 'climber' trait from earlier: you get a point roughly every ten minutes, and what can you do with it? [i]+1% vaulting speed[/i]. Other examples (per point) include: +2.5 health, +0.75% ranged damage, +1% weak spot damage, +0.5% elemental damage resistance; [i]you get my point[/i]. Sure, these upgrades add up, but they're so useless on their own and feel like a waste of time to allocate; this is something I should be looking forward to doing, but I so often found myself letting points build up to spend in bulk in the hope that I could feel any sense of improvement within my character outside of the relatively standard gear upgrades.

[h3]Final Thoughts[/h3]

Despite my criticism, I've generally started each section on a positive note, and with good reason: Remnant's innovation is a breath of fresh air within the souls-like genre that, at this point, is infamous for its formulaic and static mechanics found in every title trying to emulate Fromsoft's masterpieces. However, outside of the brilliant combat, I'm not yet convinced whether these new ideas are the next big thing for the genre or whether they should have never seen the light of day; the potential is certainly there, however, and, as a game I already recommend, I'm very keen to see how Remnant improves in the sequel later this month.

Remnant: From the Ashes is a really good game that could have been a great game if it weren't marred by its lack of attention to detail and its commitment to imitating its source inspirations rather than adapting to them.

For those unfamiliar with this game and are wondering what its all about, it's basically Dark Souls meets Warframe. The main style of game play is that of a third-person over-the-shoulder shooter with dodge rolling and fragile constitution. The world maps are randomly generated throughout each playthrough with a few consistent events that coincide with the predetermined plot line ever player will experience. This allows for pretty decent replayability and keeps things fresh when playing in another player's game world.

Generally, the game feels good to play and its fun. When the pieces fit together, it can be pretty thrilling and exciting to play. There's nothing quite like surviving an onslaught of enemies rushing you from all angles while you scrap by with what little remaining ammo you have and are masterfully avoiding damage. It's also fun to search the world for hidden secrets, such as a cool piece of armor or weapon tucked away in zones if you look hard enough for it. The game also feels really good to play with friends and that alone may be worth the price of admission.

I do take some issues with the game though, primarily how unpolished it can be at times. I'd say the biggest offender, something that many other games have also failed, is how they implemented the random level generation. It's particularly offensive in Remnant because you WILL get pretty bad Deja-vu at times. I've walked into pieces of a dungeon that have the exact same layout as a dungeon I just completed 20 minutes earlier, other times I've done dungeons that just seemed like a reversed version of another one i completed already. I've found important items in the exact same spots in the exact same generated room. Beyond the randomly generated rooms, there are also random bosses interspersed throughout each player's game world and these are always just bigger versions of other enemies you've already been fighting. It's things like this that just feel incredible lazy from the developers, it's passable enough to make the game a game, but its no where near the level of detail that you'd expect from a game who is clearly pulling inspiration from Dark Souls.

In addition, there are also a few quality of life improvements and poor design choices that I'm surprised the developers have somehow overlooked. Stuff like enemies aggroing onto you from the moment you stand up from the checkpoint crystals. Sound design is pretty bad at times, it sounds like enemies are right behind you but nothing ever shows up. You can be following the sound a monster's growls and never seem to find it because it sounds really close when in reality its not. Likewise, monsters will actually run up on you from behind but you won't hear them. This can be pretty detrimental in a game that is focusing its difficulty on how aware you are of your surroundings and how quickly you and avoid damage. There doesn't appear to be a way to view maps of zones you've already visited without actually teleporting there. Load times in the game are pretty horrendous. The menus aren't particularly use friendly, my friends and I had no idea that you could upgrade Armor because the menu kind of obscures that fact. Interacting with NPCs are pretty clunky, sometimes the dialogue doesn't activate if the NPC was in the middle of an animation when you go to talk to them. More than one person can not talk to an NPC at a time so you all have to take turns upgrading equipment. There are quests in this game but seemingly nowhere you can view your active quests from and this could be indicative of that menu problem if this option actually does exist somewhere.

You see what I'm getting at? It's riddled with small issues that could be fixed and then there are also things they should have anticipated would cause problems down the line if they invested too much time into it. For a game to truly take the design philosophies of Dark Souls to heart they would really need to focus on the quality of the experience. Bloodborne tackled Random Level generation and the dungeons felt unique and different, rarely did you immediately notice that you were playing through some of the same chunk of rooms unless you had been playing the hell out of the chalice dungeons. There were completely unique bosses in the chalice dungeons that weren't in the core game either. And everything else in those games feels solid and intentional. Remnant just feels like its trying to sell itself as a third-person shooter souls-like without promising the same quality.

I do think this game is worth the time to play with friends because its otherwise really fun. And you know what? I'm coming back to edit this review to add that I have incredibly fond memories of this game a year later. So regardless of all the things I nitpicked about it, I couldn't actually recall all of these faults because in the grand scheme of things the game is actually really fun and what it does well is what you'll remember. 

I'm hoping Remnant gets the sequel it quite frankly deserves. And I hope that sequel is incredibly polished because, if it is, you're looking at a game franchise that will be the next big thing.

[h1] My Quick Review [/h1]

[b] Pros: [/b]
[list]
    [*]Has what you'd expect from Dark Souls. Estus Flask (Dragon Heart) which is upgradable, Red Eye Crystals (bonfires), [spoiler]BOSS WEAPONS!![/spoiler], as well as a hub location to teleport back to for supplies/upgrades.
    [*]The cutscenes are amazing, as well as the voice acting! Has a lot of attention to detail within the game too.
    [*]Guns can be modded to add an active skill. Really neat system.
    [*]Death doesn't penalize you. You even go back to full ammo at the checkpoint. Don't let this fool you into thiking the game is easy though.
    [*]The Multiplayer is a seemless delight where friends on steam can easily join and leave. [b] More Importantly, Everyone Picks Up The Same Drops! [/b] Don't know many games that have that but it's really nice. When you're in range of a friend you get bonus exp and such. Friends can revive you and you have maybe a 20-30s window of opportunity.
    [*]Leveling is kind of slow when you play solo. You only have 3 traits to start with which includes Health, Stamina, and a different skill depending on your class. Playing the game you'll unlock a slew of new traits which really come in handy!
    [*]Melee weapons are used with just your LMB. Saves on having to swap to it!
[/list]
[b] Cons: [/b]
[list]
    [*][b]Friendly Fire. Melee Excluded[/b]. Mobs can hit each other though which balances out.
    [*]Map loot, from what ive seen (first 4hrs), is slightly scarce but if you look hard enough you'll come across equipment.
    [*]Finding where to go using the map or the radar is a pain in the ass.
    [*]Level design is overall bland and looks the same throughout the zone you're in. Makes it easy to get turned around.

[b] Notes: [/b]
[list]
    [*]Break wooden objects anytime you see them. You'll find a lot of resources!
    [*]Don't be too shy to use up ammo. Enemies generally drop them and you can get ammo boxes to use in a pinch as a consumable.
    [*]Very immersive souls-like game with guns and it's done really well. The dodging can seem pretty slow at first but you get used to it quickly. 
    [*]If you join the hosts game, your solo play progress will not be saved.
[/list]

[b]Overall[/b]

Bored in quarantine.  This is the best time to buy the game.  DLC is coming out on the 28th.
I played six hours in one sitting and had a blast.  Quick Pros and Cons so far.
Pros:
- Graphics, setting, atmosphere.
- Randomly generated settings encourages multiple playthroughs because you don't see every boss, weapon, armor set, dungeon, mods and more during your first run.  
- Sound design is creepy and provides a constant feeling of unease.
- Combat is fluid, intense and skill-based.
- Varied enemy types keep repetition at a minimum.
- Challenging encounters, especially during the many boss fights.
- Decent Loot.
- Survival mode is fun for a few hours.

Cons:  New Cons Added 5/4/20

I just ran across the store page for this game and can't believe I haven't ever written a review, given how many hours I've played it over the past couple of years.  Since there are so many in-depth reviews here on Steam, I'll try to keep it short.  Remnant is an extremely fun game, particularly if you like third person shooters with RPG elements and tons of unique, useful loot.  It does have a Dark Souls vibe but it's a very, very different game, and focuses on shooting rather than melee. Like DS and other similar games, it is fairly difficult, but it's certainly made easier by the fact that you don't lose your loot or progress when you die (which happens fairly often until you get the hang of it). 

The game definitely requires a wiki to get the most out of it, due to the vast number of weapons and items you can find, as well as the fact that several conditions have to align before you can get the best gear.  For me that's just part of the fun though, as I love looking stuff up and figuring out how to find it, beating the boss (or bosses) to get said weapon/item, and then finally getting to use the (usually awesome) weapon/item for the rest of the game. 

The only downside to the game, IMHO, is the level scaling mechanic.  While this often drives me away from a game, it works out OK in this one, as long as you utilize somewhat counter-intuitive leveling practices.  To clarify, if you level up your gear as quickly as the game allows during the early levels (such as you would in most games), you will end up running into enemies that are much more difficult than if you kept your gear level low.  For example, if you stay at gear level 3 or under for the entire first world, the enemies will stay at that difficulty/strength equivalent, and you'll rarely have too much trouble with the regular enemies or bosses.  However, if you level up to gear level 6-7 or higher early on, the enemies and bosses will scale with your gear level and become much more difficult.  The lesson I learned the hard way is this:  Just because your gear is stronger doesn't necessarily mean you'll be able to take on a much stronger boss.    Take my advice and level up slowly (adding appx. 3-4 levels per world).  By the end of the regular campaign, you'll be at appx. level 15-16, which has worked out really well for me throughout several character runs.  You can then level your character the rest of the way during the Subject 2923 DLC (if you're still having fun :), and finish up at the level 20 cap.  I know it's strange, but I think you'll find the game is a lot more fun with these particular tactics.

If I had to point out the best part of the game, it would be the shooting mechanics, which are some of the best in any third person game I've played.  Accuracy, fire rate, damage, and all sorts of other variables really matter when choosing a weapon, and it really keeps the game interesting.  I haven't even mentioned the trait system, which is really cool as well, and plays a huge part in your character's overall build.  Melee is secondary in this game, but does play a vital role in certain circumstances, and is still really fun to utilize as an adjunct to your ranged weapons.  

Sorry the review ended up being much longer than I planned!!!  Here's the skinny... 

TLDR:  Overall, it's a fantastic game and one of my all time favorites.  I hope you get as much enjoyment from it as I have :)

Cheers,

Remnant: From the Ashes could be described as a Lovecraftian Dark Souls with guns but that wouldn't paint a totally accurate picture. 

The major difference with Dark Souls is that it is much less punishing since you never lose any experience when you die and that's a huge difference because it means you won't be punished for pushing forward if you fail. 

The more you play, the more you will be getting ahead, collecting new items and weapons and scraps to upgrade your gear. 

This game respects your time even if you're too reckless or not patient enough to play it safe and that makes it a fun experience for players who may be frustrated with more punishing mechanics (but if that sounds too casual you can always ramp up the difficulty or play the rogue like mode that was introduced with the DLC). 

The game also rewards you for exploring the environment (quick tip, if something can be broken then you should definitely treat it as a barrel in a CRPG and break it). 

Speaking of which, the game also relies on procedural generation and that adds a lot of replay value. It is meant to be played more than once and alternatively you can even run adventures without re-rolling your campaign. 

It is 3rd person only but I've found that it can induce motion sickness in which case I would suggest disabling motion blur and using the FOV slider (that is somewhere deep in the options menu).

The game relies on autosaves so backing up your saves after every session in case  the autosave gets corrupted is a good idea. FYI saves are located in this folder: \Users\[your windows name]\AppData\Local\Remnant\Saved

I didn't care much for the dialogues in the opening area and that didn't make for a great first impression but the lore is also presented with notes and texts (and that is a lot more subtle it even left me wanting for more background and lore). I find reading about this stuff a lot more enjoyable than listening to some NPCs reciting some corny exposition that comes across as a bit cheesy (and puts your character in the shoes of the formulaic chosen one). 

I hit a wall with the first boss I met (Enchanter Shroud). Most of the time I'd say it can pay off to keep at it but in that instance I restarted and I'm glad I did. That particular boss was difficult for me because at this point I hadn't had a chance to invest in Stamina and Health and I felt overwhelmed and badly needed to adapt to different tactics (getting targeted by mobs while being shot at and targeted by area attacks was a lot). When I restarted I got a different boss and he turned out to be a pushover (at least for my playing style). Different bosses add to replay value to the game as you can imagine. 

I'm not a co-op player. I get enough interaction with people in real life and that's not how I like to play. In solo mode you can't rely on team mates to revive you and you can't count on them to distract enemies either. 

Some players say that the game can't be soloed. My reflexes are not what they used to be but on normal difficulty I'm doing ok and more importantly I'm having fun. Some bosses go down without any hassle while others take some real work but I like the fact that the game keeps me on my toes without making me complacent or making me feel like I'm wasting my time. 

It's another difference with most Souls like games. It's a lot more relaxed and you know that the more you play, the more you increase your character's traits and the more you experience a sense of growth and progression. 

One thing that can be misleading right at the start is when the game asks you to pick up a class. It does seem like a huge choice but in truth the difference is rather superficial. The gear other classes get can be acquired at the very beginning of the game and it's only the starting points that differ a bit. They also get different weapon mods (special magic like abilities) but you can purchase them as well. The only significant difference is the starting trait (I would recommend Ex Cultist for the only reason that the Spirit Trait improves the use of mods and that's probably a lot more useful in order to use special abilities more often). You can still get the traits from the other classes but that may take much longer. 

I didn't comment on the music and the visuals. There is a really strong atmosphere and the sounds really help with that. The creature design keeps reminding me of creatures from the Cthulhu Mythos and that's definitely a plus. The game is Lovecraftian in many ways and I won't get into spoiler territory but if you're at all familiar with the Dreamlands in Lovecraft's writing you will probably enjoy the lore the game has to offer. 

All in all it's a game that I would heartily recommend to players who like the idea of a challenging third person shooter with a great atmosphere especially if they don't have the patience (or the time) for more punishing mechanics.

Remnant is not only one of those games where it's difficult to find concise information on what it's actually like, but also whose reviews tend to be either written by fanboys or people who hate it because it's not actually Dark Souls.  

It basically feels like a stripped down Fallout influenced by Dark Souls, mixed with a Stargate theme and some weird fantasy mechanics that are never explained.  There you go.  

Is it like Dark Souls?  Saving you some technical explanations, it's more forgiving in terms of mechanics.  Bosses are interesting, but sub-par and surrounded by "adds".  I did appreciate that many of them have an alternate kill which results in a completely different item drop. They also have unskippable cutscenes, which is unforgivable in a grinding game.  Regular enemies are a dime a dozen with heavy telegraphing, and the very snappy control system feels wasted on them. 

The story and lore are pretty intriguing, and then suddenly it's over.  They also didn't bother having an actual ending, unless you count the pseudo-ending provided by the DLC Subject 2923.  Sidequests are practically non-existent.  Character interactions are brief, and shallow.

Levels are randomly generated, but honestly pretty short.  At any given time you can roll a world via "Adventure Mode", which cycles everything, completely outside the campaign.  If you're thorough, there are very, VERY few items (I only recall one) that are missable in the campaign, but if you do, you can reroll that as well.  Not every boss, character, piece of gear or event is available on every roll.  

There are, technically, no character builds.  Your starter gear is affected by one of three classes, but through various achievements or events in the game you acquire cards with various effects.  These Traits level up to 20 a piece, and there are 50 of them, ranging from HP steal, to armor effectiveness, melee damage, some stats, all sorts of things.  All of them are active at the same time from the moment you acquire them.

The gear count is 49 weapons, 18 armor sets, 74 rings (of which you can wear two at a time), and 36 amulets in the game.  There are also 40 weapon mods providing your functional abilities, but not every weapon can change the slotted mod.  Weapons and armor have their own levels, gained from a small set of materials you find on your travels.  Weapon mods have their own stat increases based on the level of the weapon that they're on, and recharge as you do damage with them (or just naturally, via specific loadouts).

Remnant semi-fails on its RNG and replay value.  While the core game is fun, and the 3-person coop has reasonable scaling, it's largely a collection game.  This is because the story is so short, enemies do not scale in such a way that they require specific builds, AND loot remains the same on all difficulties except Hardcore and Survival modes.  Remnant is something you "just play."  This is fine for many people, but if you expect to need a variety of equipment and/or abilities to get through sections of the game, you will be utterly disappointed.  "Advanced challenges" don't exist.  

In Hardcore mode, you create a fresh character for a perma-death run for the campaign, in order to snag one of ten pieces of account-bound equipment or an emote.  Any unlocks are saved after completion of the entire campaign, or death, for any and all characters.

In Survival mode you are stripped to your undies, taken to a room to buy some randomized starter gear, and have to beat a random world from its beginning that also has randomized gear and trait drops.  When you complete it or die trying, you're chucked back out to the starter room, with any unlocks being account-bound like Hardcore mode.  Five of the ten unique items dropped here can also be bought in the regular game with a special resource gained from any difficulty other than normal.  

Since item drops, character appearances (such as vendors), or specific dungeons are random, the RNG can be quite horrendous in spite of the relatively small environments.  I gave up on a particular armor set after thirty or forty rolls on a particular world.  It doesn't help that none of it is necessary to get through the game, and some builds are dead in the water depending purely on how many times you can do things like looking for an insect in a random room, in a random dungeon that has a random chance to spawn IN A RANDOM PLACE ON THE MAP.  Even with good friends, good music, possibly good booze, that kind of sh*t is just too much.  

Good game, get it on sale, yes you want the DLC, just don't expect to blow hundreds of hours on it.

I had originally written this game off because I saw various articles about people saying this game wasn’t designed for solo play. Recently, I was running out of new games to play, so I decided to give this game a shot. I am so glad that I did because in my opinion, this game is on the level of Dark Souls 3, Bloodborne, and Sekiro, some of my all-time favorite games.

So let's tackle the complaint that originally turned me off from playing this game: that this isn't designed for solo play. Welp, I beat this game on Hard completely solo. Not only is this game completely playable solo only, it's a genuinely fun experience playing solo. I think the main reason it can seem like this game isn't designed for solo play is because you're always fighting multiple enemies at once, including boss fights (i.e. multiple bosses or 1 boss and infinite enemy adds). So it seems like you need multiple people so that, for example, 1 person can focus on the boss while another player can take care of the adds. While I am sure this can make things easier, you don't NEED this. Everything is designed such that 1 player can handle multiple enemies all at once in a fair manner:
	• When exploring out in the wild/dungeons, enemies will almost always be in front of you. In the rare instances where enemies spawn behind you (usually elites), a sound will play so that you can tell that this has happened and deal with it accordingly (i.e. it's never a cheap surprise)
	• For the most part, enemies don't just automatically spawn in boss fights. Bosses actually summon them. This means you can tell when enemies are about to spawn AND the boss is pre-occupied with summoning the enemies (i.e. since summoning is a "move", the boss can't attack you). This means that you can take out a large portion of the adds before the boss starts attacking you again.
	• Again, while this can be called a "Souls-like", you typically don't die in 2-3 hits (…..except for boss hits). Depending on the enemy it can take them like 4-6 hits before they kill you. So if an add hits you while exploring or during a boss fight, it's not the end of the world.

Point is, through excellent design decisions, the developers have totally made this game be a challenging and enjoyable experience for solo play.

With that out of the way, how's the gameplay? The gameplay can be divided into 2 parts: general exploration and boss fights. When you're out and about exploring the world, you're going to be facing "normal" enemies and "elite" enemies. Normal enemies provide almost no challenge and can be easily killed at range before they even come close to you. Even if they do hit you, it takes 4-6 hits from these enemies to kill you. So if you're just facing normal enemies, the game is really easy. However, every so often, you'll come across elite enemies. These enemies are like bosses but with much less health. They can kill you in 2-3 hits and can withstand a bit of punishment. They'll definitely be able to attack you 1-3 times before you're able to take them down. 

So basically, a lot of the enemies are similar to Dark Souls. However, Remnant makes the enemies a lot more difficult to fight than they typically would be by adding 2 elements:
	1. Various enemies have guns themselves. So they can shoot bullets at you which you can't dodge.
	2. Enemies have much higher aggro range and can spawn close to each other.

Having said the above, you can just imagine how difficult it would be to face down like 4 enemies with pistols coming at you while a tanky elite enemy with a greatsword is charging you. So you have to make sure you're not caught in these types of situations, which requires you to come to each battle well prepared. For example, you may want to use a sniper rifle to pick off enemies from far away. Or maybe the level design is too constricted for that (e.g. in a cave) so you want to equip a close-ranged, fast firing weapon instead so that you can kill swarms of enemies quickly. You also have to factor in the magazine size and reload speed of the weapons. There are a lot of tools at your disposal, and it's up to you to use them effectively. This is in stark contrast to Dark Souls where you simply need a fast weapon for bosses and maybe a slow but long ranged weapon (e.g. ultra great sword) for regular enemies.

While I would say fighting regular enemies in Remnant is more engaging than in Dark Souls, I feel the bosses are clearly better in Dark Souls. This is because bosses in Remnant have like 3-5 moves, apart from a few exceptions. The bosses in Dark Souls can have like 5-10 moves. So the bosses in Dark Souls are a lot more complex and difficult. Correspondingly, you get a much bigger feeling of achievement when you beat them. The main reason bosses in Remnant are difficult is because of the numerous adds that spawn in almost every single boss battle. While this is definitely difficult, I personally prefer the difficulty that comes from a lone boss that's complex to master.

One thing I'll give to Remnant is that unlike Dark Souls, you have to be a lot more aware of level design. In Dark Souls, you simply go up to the boss and start dodging. In Remnant, you can't do that because then you'll be surrounded by the boss and its adds. So you have to find places in the level that either provide you with cover or ensure that all the enemies will spawn directly in front of you (e.g. by running to a place with a wall at your back and sides). For example, in one particular boss fight I was having a lot of trouble until I realized I should run to the right part of the level instead of the left part of the level since there's more cover on the right side. So I'll give it to Remnant. This is the first Souls-like that made me consider the level design as part of my strategy to beat bosses.

The progression system in Remnant is fairly decent. You slowly unlock new weapons (you can equip a long gun, a secondary gun, and a melee weapon), armor, necklaces, and rings (you can equip 2). New weapons can significantly change how you handle enemies, so they're always exciting to find. Armor has set bonuses, so the decision to what armor you can wear in this game is more than just about poise/fashion….. Although in my opinion all the armor in Remnant looks ugly :P. The effects from the jewelry can be pretty significant and you can make entire builds around them once you find a few that work together. There are also weapon mods in this game. Each weapon can be equipped with 1 mod. These are basically magic abilities that can provide a passive boost, summon allies to fight for you, provide a burst of damage, etc… The weapon mods recharge by dealing damage to enemies. So they help to change up the gameplay and ensure it doesn't get stale.

There's also a trait point system. As you play Remnant, you'll unlock trait points by either gaining experience or finding books strewn about randomly in the world. Traits provide passive bonuses like increased critical chance, increased reload speed, resistance to ranged attacks, etc… You will not be able to max out your traits in 1 playthrough, so it's something nice to look forward to and gives you another reason to do multiple playthroughs.

Speaking of multiple playthroughs, this game is designed pretty decently for it. Whenever you create a new campaign, the game decides which dungeons and bosses you'll be facing. It's impossible to go to every single dungeon and face every single boss in 1 playthrough. So playing through the campaign again will likely provide you with an entirely new experience because you'll be facing new enemy placements, dungeons, and bosses.

Overall, I really enjoyed my time playing this game. I was skeptical of a Dark Souls with guns, but I am glad to be proven wrong. Hopefully there'll be a sequel :)

The core game is to shoot demon-like enemies while traversing a map from point A to B. Even if this game just seems like a simple concept it has a wining randomizing twist. 

[h1]Imagine a simple shooter but better[/h1]
Yes there is a storyline, shops and crafting but what makes it enjoyable is that the items, maps and enemies are randomized on each playthrough. Even the bosses appear in a somewhat randomized way. it's very unlikely to have the same experience say in two different runs in a row. 

[h2]GamePlay[/h2]
it's simple, shoot, dodge, take cover, heal, and buff and even make summons to help you. Gun handling feel ok but not too special. Nothing is bad it's not to the levels of what a AAA game like Doom. The multiplayer adds a lot to the replayability and fun factor. Drop-in drop-out coop makes it easy to join games. 

[b]The challenge[/b]
The standard enemy variation make encounters feel unique a lot of the time. They all behave differently depending on the type. They will take cover and will attack in groups to take you down while others will run and take cover. They even have multiple attacks so that you will not feel too comfortable around them. Boss fights are more engaging, dealing with enemies in a arena type map and dealing with boss powers. The game can be a grind after you finished the campaign but the levels are fun to redo. The game has 4 difficulty levels and 2 game modes (3 with the DLC).

[b]Loot[/b]
Most of the loot gathered from enemies are crafting materials for weapon upgrades. So I won't categorize this as a loot shooter. Other types of loot consist of accessories and weapons but they appears very sparingly in some maps or after bosses. After some events your will be awarded traits use the to boost your character like increase damage or speed just to name a few. 

[h2]Graphics and Audio[/h2]
The 3 biomes or worlds look all very unique and very nice. For example, in the city the layout appears like in an urban area you can see a mix of towering buildings mixed with smaller ones. They are connected by streets or passages that leads into abandoned offices, sewers, etc. There is a foreboding theme of weird and end of times look and feel. Weapons and character armor are portrayed very nicely and feel in the right place in this world. 

The Music does an ok job. A bit forgettable but works in this game. Sound effects are nice but can become repetitive after a while.

[h2]Critisism[/h2]
As for other negatives, a big one I found is the loot system is not engaging. After you get the weapons you want to upgrade will will spend most of your time upgrading it instead of experimenting with other ones. Getting a new weapon was never exciting because my main one was way more powerful.

[h2]In the end[/h2]
I played for a lot more than I tough I would. It reminds me of Dark Souls mixed with Fallout. If you like these games I suggest you take a look at [url=https://store.steampowered.com/app/617290/Remnant_From_the_Ashes/]Remnant: From the Ashes[/url]

This game is often misunderstood as "Dark Souls With Guns" where that really is the furthest thing from the truth. Remnant: From the Ashes is a robust Sci-Fi Shooter that has you traversing a series of unique planets as you work toward your goal of finding a man called Ford. As you kill bosses, and complete events, you equip your character with guns, armor, and weapon mods that all have a huge impact on how you play. 

However, the game shines most brilliantly in Adventure Mode, and while paying for what I feel should have been a free update - Swamps of Corsus in Adventure Mode - is unfortunate, the price is well worth it, if you have the spending cash to burn. 

Grinding Adventure Mode will allow you to roll through a specific planet as many times as you want, to grind for resources, items, and loot. Personally, this is where I spend most of my time in the game. 

Survival was an amazing add, as well. It's fast-paced, and challenging, but I did wish they fleshed out the game mode a little bit, and offered some sort of progression rewards. In fact, Survival Mode could be a game in and of itself, if there was more long-term progression in the mode. 

Overall, if you are expecting "Dark Souls With Guns" go download the Dark Souls gun mods. If you want a dynamic Sci-Fi third person shooter with serious replayability and rogue-like elements, this is the game for you.

This game has literally zero cheat protection. Read on for why that's a problem even in a coop game. 

If you hit the 'random join' button (which is the only way to join other games) you can and will be dropped into games where people have hacked their game with infinite money and trait points. Those will be applied to your game without warning, and without the ability to revert those cheats in your own game.

I.E. if you randomly join other games for coop, which is your only method to join other games (assuming you don't have 2 friends to play premade groups) then eventually your save is guaranteed to be max-leveled by someone hacking their game.

I had this happen twice in one day, causing me to have all traits unlocked with max trait points along with near infinite money and crafting materials.

The game itself is a ton of fun, and well worth playing, but given that the developers don't care whatsoever about anti-cheat you're on your own when (not if) your save is maxed out joining random players.

I can't recommend a game that thinks that's ok, and I'm a person that isn't even dead set against people hacking their own games however they want. The fact it unlocks on my save without any warning or ability to undo those changes means that this game effectively has no challenge, which is the core concept of the game. 

This review will remain negative until some sort of mechanic is put in place to mitigate the already rampant hacking in this title. 

At the moment, your only option if this happens is to delete your save and start over. That's not a real solution.

EDIT: 

Someone kindly provided advice on how to manually back up saves in case this happens to you in the comments. I had to disable comments due to this review being bombed by misinformation and personal attacks, but this information should also be available on the Steam or official forums, or the official discord.

I find that solution to be inadequate and was already aware of it, but it probably bears mentioning since it could potentially help others with the game should they buy it.

I was on the fence on this game for a few months; the last time I played a coop [i]Soulslike[/i] game I was immediately disappointed. However, [i]Remnant: From the Ashes[/i] plays great and obviously tries its best to not skirt [i]too[/i] close to the things that have influenced it.

The game is a post apocalyptic shooter that plays like a pretty loose mix of [i]Dark Souls[/i] and [i]Gears of War[/i], just without [i]Gears[/i]' heavy focus on taking cover. Players (up to three can play coop together) carry a main rifle, a sidearm, and a melee weapon while poppin' these tree demon/zombies called the "Root". The game is about 1/3 small enemy combat, 1/3 boss fights and 1/3 looting, leveling and exploration. The areas are fairly straight-forward, and it's the combat that is the main draw. The game offers an assortment of weapons and a healthy variety of enemies all the way to the end of the campaign.

Gameplay is reminiscent of [i]Soulslike[/i] games in that there's attacking and dodging. The majority of the game focuses on gunplay which is decent enough, and there are even some basic melee weapons in the mix that don't really outshine the likes of [i]Dark Souls[/i] in variety, but achieve the same basic mechanics: you swing at stuff a few times to kill it. Guns end up being a much more palatable bread n' butter sort of combat for this kind of approach, and the game ends up mixing in its' brand of spells, called "mods", rather well. Active AoE/team buffs, "attack" spells and summoned helpers are the sorts of abilities you can expect during the game.

The game is difficult, and there is often times no obvious way to "cheese" out of a boss. You aren't expected to collect your remains with each death, but some bosses are pretty unforgiving when it comes to mistakes. Shortcomings in player skill can be made up for by acquiring passive skills, called "traits", from doing particular things in the game. There are no "classes" in the game, and despite the game starting out presenting something that appears to look that way, characters can (fully) level passives to push their playing level a bit further.

The campaign mode runs players through a 10-20 hour campaign depending on your level of exploration, competency, etc. However, what isn't apparent in a single run is that the game is fairly randomized. The world is constructed from blocks, which includes some side-dungeons that aren't integral to the main game. These dungeons, however, sometimes have bosses and rewards of their own, so you [i][b]will not[/b][/i] see 100% of the game on a single run. Good news is, however, that there are modes that help support players that don't want to run through the entire stretch of the game to reroll parts of the game. There is an "adventure mode", where "chapter" content can be replayed independently of the story aspects of the game. This is especially handy, as while the story isn't complete garbage, it's also not great enough that you'd probably replay the game to rewatch. The last mode is "survival" mode, which is more appropriately described as "roguelite" mode. In that mode, the player begins with just a single sidearm, earning and buying equipment and powers as they go through dungeons that increase in difficulty as time goes on.

The game is a lot more forgiving in a coop setting, and arguably more fun considering most [i]Soulslike[/i] games also copy the off-kilter style of coop the genre has been known to include (or exclude entirely). It allows for three players to join up, which share everything aside from individual ammo pickups, so it's a fairly relaxed experience when it comes to loot (except in the DLC "Survival" mode, which everything but scrap is split). 

In terms of aesthetics, the game is fairly competent. The game is does a good job in enemy, equipment, player character and world design. Lip sync is a little scary, and there not [i]everything[/i] has a unique representation in the world (some "mods" for example, share "skins" on the weapons), but it's more than serviceable.

If you're looking for a more blatant [i]Soulslike[/i] that has a focus on gunplay instead of fantasy melee/ranged/spells, give [i]Remnant[/i] a go, especially if you're looking for a game that has up to three player coop, or are looking for a game with a decent roguelite mode with good coop support.

At the time of writing this I've been playing Remnant for over 300 hours including hardcore runs, extensive survival runs and finishing the game and DLCs on every difficulty. Needless to say this game will geta  positive review from me, however if you've never played the game and want to know if this game is or isn't for you this review may be helpful to you.

Let's start with the things Remnant isn't. Remnant isn't a linear shooter that focusses heavily on story and cinematics. However it isn't an open world looter shooter either. The closest thing I can think of when describing this game is a Soulslike with guns and semi randomized maps à la Diablo. If you're expecting a gripping story or a new weapon drop every couple of minutes you'll be dissapointed. So who is this game actually for? Well let me just tell you about my experience with Remnant.

Playing through the entire game for the first time took me about 20 hours or so. Keep in mind I'm a player who takes his time when playing a game, often stopping to look at a beautiful scenary or to listen to a games sound track. I only managed to beat the game on normal back then (the easiest difficulty) so sure enough I wanted a second run, this time with a higher difficulty. Once that was done I wanted all the items the game has to offer, however some of them would only drop in hardcore mode. I wasn't good enough for that yet since it requires you to beat bosses on your first try so I went with nightmare difficulty and Apocalype difficulty next until I was good enough to not get killed 40 times by the same boss. I also played survival mode and adventure mode to fullfill my second goal, hunting down all the achievements which include killing 10 bosses in a row on survival mode and defeating a wolrd boss without taking a single point of dmg. 

So what kept me entertained during all these numerous runs? It certainly couldn't have been the rudimentary and disjointed story that's mostly told via diary entries and item descriptions. Maybe it was the huge amount of loot I was showered with? Well no there's quite few armorsets, guns, modifications (skills), traits (passives) and rings to find. But certainly nowhere near the level of borderlands or Diablo. So what really made me play the game over and over was the fantastic gunplay. Remnant has hands down the best gunplay I have ever played in a shooter game. Movement is fluid an precise. Every weapon feels drastically different and fun to use. From a standard "fire a fast as you can click" pistol to a "this shotgun banishes enemies into a different dimension" Remnant has everything. There's not a single weapon that is not fun to use or doesn't handle well. Landing hits in this game feels incredibly satisfying. Even on higher difficulties precise heashots will quickly down enemies. Only a few minibosses fall into the category "bullet sponge" but they are deliberately designed that way. You can stagger most enemies, making them cancel attacks or spells in the process. Shooting them in different body parts often has drastically different outcomes. Eg. shooting a huge enemy in the knee might cause them to fall over and faceplant right in front of you. Shoot a weaker enemy in the chest from close range and they'll be knocked off their feet. A caster is doing something you don't like? Well if you hit them in the face they might just stop whatever it is they were doing and run away.

Generelly speaking the enemy design in this game is fantastic. The AI is smart and enemies often work in synergies. Every enemy has multiple movesets which the player needs to memorize if they don't want to die quickly. Even after hundreds hours of gameplay I still occasionally see new moves from enemies I've never seen before like a caster that I though was only ranged hitting at me with his staff when I got too close to him. The fantastic gunplay is perfected by so called "weapon mods". These are basically spells that range from a standard flamethrower, to conjuring swarms of insects to summoning radiocative flying skulls. Once you are familiar with the weapon you're using and the enemies your facing you will find youself skillfully dodging enemies while keeping a close track on your mod coldowns, while listening to audio cues indicating attacks happening outside if your field of view and analyzing enemy movement patters to anticipate the next attack. It's challening, fast paced, brutal and incredibly satisfying. It's this kind of gameplay flow that made me continue playing the game even when the story was done and my character had found most the items availbeable in the game.

In closing I also want to quickly mention the graphics and sound of this game which I think are both phenomenal. I work as a professional 3D character artist and as a result I like to pay close attention to enemy and environmental design. Remnant doesn't have photorealistic textures, face scans or environmental assets  created through photogrammetry. But what it does have is a phenomenal art direction. There is more creativity put into each of Remnants 5 worlds than you'll see in most other games. It doesn't matter if you encounter some Giger-esque, biomechanical monstrosities in the desert of Rhom, insectoid zombies on Corsus or whimsical satyr creatures with elaborate facemasks in Yaesha. Everything in this game is beautiful to look at, The silhouettes, color palettes and sheer variety of visual languages is astounding. This is the kind of artdirection that impresses me when playing a game and has been another factor, next to the excellent gameplay, why I could play this game for hundreds of hours. As for the sound design not only is there a huge library of unique sounds that build athmosphere and add to the visceral feel of combat. But most sounds are also cleverly interwoven into the gameplay serving as audio cues that help you keep track of enemy positions and predict their attacks even when they are out of sight. It's only when you get blinded by a ratman-magician in Reisum and have to play with almost zero vision for a couple of seconds that you realize you could play this game almosty blindly because the sound design is so well done. Add some absolutely fantastic bossfight music too (Haarsgard) and you'll get why I enjoy Remnants sound design so much.

Last but not least I have to talk about bossifghts and difficulty. Similar to other souls like games there are a lot of bossfights in this game too. Some bosses focus on quick reactions/muscle memory and being able to read their next attack in a split second. Others will turn half the arena into "the floor is lava". There's summoner bosses swarming the arena with trash mobs. Dual bosses which attack as a team, and so on and so forth. Personally I enjoy every bossfight. They are a mayor positive for me in the game and the elf queen bossfight is still my favorite bossfight of all time (took me about 4-5 hours to beat her on nightmare before they slightly nerfed her dmg). There's also alternative kills for many of the worldbosses which will result in different movesets and item rewards. I have read however that a lot of people dislike how a lot of bosses will come with an endless spawn of minions. So keep that in mind when thinking about buying this game. 

As far as difficulty is concerned Remnant is definitely on the harder side. While I have beaten the game on the  highest difficulty and know most enemies very well I still wouldn't stand a chance on a fresh hardcore character in apocalypse difficulty and I also woudn't make it really far in apocalypse survival runs. So there's always a bigger challenge if you really want to. For beginners I would recommend you only play this game if failure motivates you instead of frustrating you. There are a couple of noob-filters early on and if you have a problem spending 20-40 tries to beat a boss you might want to give this game a pass. However if you like challenges I recommend buying this game.

I would recommend this game. I've garnered 26 hours with the past few days because I can't put the game down. The gameplay loop is pleasing, simple, rewarding, and challenging all in one.

Your first time playing is going to be through the story. It is SHORT, but intentionally so, and I'll explain that in a bit. The lore is surprisingly interesting. It's not always well written, and about half of the characters are a bit bland, but the ideas they're conveying are really intriguing to me. There's lore to read from terminals and journals around the world and it's a big multiverse-like concept that was well developed. I'm not going to spoil anything here, obviously, but if you're a lore buff you'll probably enjoy stirring the concepts of the story in your head, if you at least don't enjoy the writing.

Now, the gameplay. After you finish the story, you can replay it, or go through adventure mode for specific areas. And the reason you'd want to replay through the story or areas is because there's multiple bosses to spawn for certain parts of the quest, usually with two different ways to defeat them to receive different rewards (which result in new weapons or mods). After you beat them once in the story, you can't go back and defeat them again, so replaying the fights is the only way to max out your arsenal.

The maps will spawn randomly as well. They'll puzzle big sections together randomly (think Diablo) which lead to different areas each time. New optional bosses, puzzles to do, or small quests to complete for these new areas. You'll be rewarded new weapons, armor, and mods.

And what makes this all the better is that grouping up and joining other people's worlds is only to your benefit, as opposed to slugging along boringly trying to carry your friend to your level or vice versa. Because it will open up new bosses or ways to defeat bosses that you haven't done previously, allowing you to be rewarded as opposed to punished for helping a friend out. The game solves the "helping my friend grind to my point is boring" dilemma perfectly.

Speaking of co-op, co-op makes the game easier (and more fun) as you and your friends can build yourselves up around a specific composition, or just all go full on glass cannon DPS and shred the shit out of everything. Taking turns garnering aggro and using your positioning to abuse enemies' weak spots is great. It reminds me a lot of when I did WoW raids, the communication you sometimes have to pull off for bosses can be quite similar.

Gameplay involves using dodging for i-frames while abusing enemy downtime to whip in some DPS. Dodge, attack, dodge, attack, etc. The skill ceiling seems to be high for timing dodges and knowing the time to commit to DPS as opposed to playing defensively. so there is a lot of celebration to be had when you successfully beat a boss for the first time. Or the second time, on a harder difficulty.

Overall, I'm having a blast. The game has a lot of completionist gameplay for someone like me (maxing out all guns, armor, traits) so I can see myself playing for a while.

[h1] Overview [/h1]
[b]Remnant: From The Ashes[/b] (RFTA) is a hybrid between a traditional 3rd person Shooter RPG, such as [i]The Division[/i], and the Souls-like genre. Set in a time when [b]an inter-dimensional plague known as the Root devastated Earth[/b] and other worlds, players will be tasked in finding a way to stop it, and in doing so [b]traverse many strange, dangerous dimensions[/b] and planets, looking for the truth about not only the Root, but also their hidden destiny.

This mixture of genres plays out surprisingly well, [b]taking many elements characteristic of Souls games[/b]: rolls with i-frames, replenish-able healing items, map shortcuts, bonfires, material-based gear upgrading system, special boss items, and plenty of secret areas where to find unique loot or puzzles. The Souls-like part is not predominant though, [b]as many elements from traditional RPG-FPS also are significant[/b] in the gameplay, such as upgrading Traits (passives) to build a specialized character, enemy scaling based on gear level, or equipping the right sets, weapons, and mods, which grant active skills charged by dealing damage, that best suit your class' purpose.

Solo or in co-op, players will have to traverse various areas filled with enemies and loot, first on Earth and then in other alien worlds. Each zone has a "main path" to follow, and [b]several secondary dungeons[/b]. Because of [b]random generation, bosses, area types, and secondary dungeons as well are different every play-through[/b]. As a consequence, each player can end up with different boss weapons, items, and gear pieces compared to others, because [b]their worlds are different[/b]. Of course playing together in the same world means [b]getting the same gear[/b]. This mechanic boosts replay-ability by a lot, with the chance of finding what was missed in the previous run, and [b]since there are three difficulties to clear[/b], that is good.

On the bad side, it has to be said that [b]boss fights, in general, are rather underwhelming[/b] as they rely more upon spamming tons of trash mobs to create difficulty, rather than having better boss design themselves. Other than this, optimization is not very good, with slow-downs even on high-end builds in certain areas, nothing too serious. The fact [b]some mods or weapons are much more powerful than others, and because of RNG they can be missed[/b], unbalances the late-game phases a bit, especially against the final boss, where specific mods and weapons are fundamental. Level design is also not the best, [b]with places looking all too similar to each other[/b].

[b]I suggest this game to any Souls fans, and also to who enjoyed games such as [i]The Division[/i], meaning TPS-RPGs[/b]. Offering about [b]16-18 hours of content for one run[/b], with three difficulties to clear, good replay-ability, [b]i can suggest full price purchase to fans of either genre that also have a team to play with[/b], while players just curious are better off waiting for at least a small sale.

[h1] Pros & Cons [/h1]

🔵 [b] Pros [/b]
+ Successful mix of souls-like elements and 3rd person RPG, creating a satisfying, challenging and fun gameplay experience. 
+ Three difficulties, combined with RNG world generation, boost replay-ability by a lot while also making it different, and not just the "usual grind" of the exact same content.
+ Excellent art direction and graphics, offering evocative landscapes, beautiful environments consistently.
+ Good amount of gear, weapons, accessories and passives, to build classes suitable for any play-style with a high degree of freedom.

🔴 [b] Cons [/b]
- Most bosses have sub-par design, relying mostly on trash mob spam to create difficulty, rather than better mechanics.
- Level design lacks verticality, and is rather generic, repetitive: every path and area looks very similar to others, to the point of players getting lost because of it.
- Some gear pieces are under-powered, gimmicky or useless, could use a balance rework.


[h1] In-Depth Breakdown [/h1]

🎮 [b]Gameplay Analysis [/b]
The gameplay of [b]RFTA[/b] is divided into Exploration, Character Management and Combat.

[b]Exploration[/b] goes through linear levels, containing a main path with several bosses for each zone, then several secondary dungeons, which can as well contain bosses, arenas, puzzles, or other special areas from which players can get unique loot, additional XP, or quest items. Levels are randomized for each player's world, and so are the secondary dungeon types, areas, and bosses found. There is a good amount of secrets, hidden items to find for the keen of sight, so exploring deeply every zone is strongly encouraged. Some NPCs can be met during travels, many of which turn out to be merchants, selling unique loot, crafting materials, and even triggering quests at times. Most found Crystals (bonfires) can be used as fast-travel points to-and-from your base, where all traders and upgrade facilities reside.

[b]Character Management[/b] consists in upgrading, swapping and modding weapons, gear pieces and accessories in order to best optimize your hero for a role, such as DPS, Tank, and so on. This is done mainly at the Ward, base of operations, where several traders offer upgrading and selling of new gear, mods and accessories. Materials gathered in the world, such as Iron types or unique boss materials, can be used to improve gear or craft new ones. Trait points, gained with XP from killing enemies, quests, are used to upgrade passive abilities giving more Stamina, Resistance to specific damage types, and many other bonuses. Respec is available, but only after finishing the game the first time, as a consumable. Generally, building a specialized character with a given role is better than a jack of all trades, and since there are no usage requirement for weapons, abilities or mods, players have more build freedom. Mods power scales with weapon upgrade level, growing as the weapon they are fitted inside of does.

[b]Combat[/b] is the core of RFTA, and plays out in a very souls-like fashion, where learning enemy attack patterns, dodging at the right time, learning how to use i-frames, and generally being careful about even the lowest of enemy peons, are all fundamental mechanics, especially at higher difficulties. Teamwork is essential, especially in boss fights, where some players take care of trash mobs while others dedicate only to damaging the boss. Soloing bosses and areas is also possible given the scaling system, but ultimately harder. The various damage types (fire, radiation, bleeding, etc.) from both players and bosses, with relative weaknesses or resistances and status effects, give more depth to the system, having players keep multiple damage type weapons for different situations. Consumables are very important in getting rid of said status effects, long-lasting and crippling most of the time. Overall, the combat of RFTA is a serious challenge, and generally is satisfying for both souls-fans and TPS-RPG players. 


🔩 [b] Performance Analysis [/b]
Some areas have slowdowns even on high-end systems, but generally the performance is acceptable without many major issues to report. No crashes or major bugs to report. [Ryzen 9 3900X, RTX 2080Ti, 32GB RAM DDR4].

[h1] Final Thoughts [/h1]
Overall, RFTA is definitely [b]a solid co-op shooter that blends elements from different genres successfully[/b], creating an ultimately satisfying and challenging gameplay formula.
