Game has pros, game has cons. I'm bordering a negative recommendation, but the execution of the game is good and the cons are part of the game design, so it relies heavily on what one whether those cons are a dealbraker for you.

The pros
1) Game is polished, animations are smooth 
2) the gameplay is cool, weapons feel good, basic mechanics are fine 
3) Visual design is cool, different zones have a unique feel.

Cons
The main thing about the game is that the map is generated for every playthrough, or if you want you can even reset the map before you finish the playthrough. In order to keep this interesting, one playthrough may have completely different bosses, and other instances. Generally speaking one zone is spread across a few maps, and on these maps you have mini-dungeons that can be a NPC, bossfight, wave defense and maybe something else.
This game relies extremely on replay value, but I think the replay value is low.

1) the bosses are cool looking, fun to do once, but mechanically they are not interesting. Almost all of them rely on adds spawning behind you, and honestly this feels really cheap.

2) the enemy variety is way too low. Between the zones, the same enemy arch-types can be found. The thing that rushes you, the thing that throws something to you, the big enemy that charges you and is tanky. In the end, the first zones of the game turns out to be a barebones version of the last zone. From a gameplay perspective, this makes replaying all these zones incredibly stupid.

3) Items can be found on the open map, and in the mini-dungeons. After the first playthrough, it's a complete gamble whether there is anything worth getting. In the open map you have to look in the more obscure places, but since I already see no real reason to be in those zones, I don't feel like shooting copy pasted enemies all over the map just to find out there is nothing to gain, or a mini-dungeon or boss that I have already done (can't get items twice).
Neither is there any guarantee that I'll get new content, or the content I "want". Let's say it turns out there is a cool weapon as part of a mini-dungeon in the last zone. There is no way knowing if it's there until you arrive at the last zone and check all locations for mini-dungeons.

4) The Leveling, items and RPG elements are pretty pointless. You level up, and this gives a trait point. There is basic traits based on what class you choose in the beginning, and other traits unlock as the game progresses, which is pretty cool honestly. However the traits themselves don't influence playstyle. They are essentially quality of life things such as higher reload speed, increased crit chance, more stamina, faster use of items.

I spend a lot of time talking about the negatives, so I want to stress that the positive points are still just as valid. To put it to an end, I think it is sad that most bosses rely on mobs for the "difficulty", and it's sad to find out that although the zones are cool and unique, the enemies found on the open map are extremely same-y across all zones. Nevertheless, it was a good amount of fun to play through the game, took me just over 10 hours to reach the final boss exploring all the content.
I don't see myself enjoying another playthrough, the game lacks the excellence in enemy design and RPG elements and I personally do not think it's worth it to plough all maps in search for all items or encounters the game has to offer.

[i]Remnant: From the Ashes[/i] is much more interesting than I expected. A lot of people call it "[i]Dark Souls[/i] with guns" and there are definitely some comparisons, but it's more than that.

The first thing to say right away is that the game has a variety of biomes that you unlock as you progress through the main story. When you go to a biome, the overall map is semi-randomized. It is [b]not[/b] procedural generation though. In fact, the map is split up into sections that were already handcrafted/pre-made by the developers. The only aspect that is randomized is which sections appear in your run-through of the biome, and also which mini-boss and boss you fight.

Certain parts of the maps have side quests or various NPCs to meet, some of which will give you new equipment or special upgrades. And if you haven't seen everything for a biome, then you are able to re-roll it, so it might reveal some of the areas you haven't seen yet. The only downside to this is that there are a few special events where you need the biome to pick multiple areas in the same run, but that's only if you're trying to do all of the side content. Plus, you can re-roll early if you want to.

The main story starts off somewhat generically but I think by the end of the game, it definitely has some interesting notes, and the final boss is fun. The game has two DLCs, the first of which isn't exactly the best but it contains probably the toughest boss fight of the entire game. The second DLC ends up continuing the main storyline with an even better wrap-up, in my opinion, and covers the lore much more strongly; though your interest depends upon whether you're intrigued by the world.

Combat is very smooth and the best part of the game. The weapons also have a good amount of variety. You carry two guns and one melee weapon at a time, though you can swap things out as you see fit. Also, the game is actually easier than [i]Dark Souls[/i] when it comes to dying because you don't actually lose anything. All you do is revive back at the last crystal you interacted with. That's not to say the game is easy overall, as there are definitely some tough spots. The bosses as a whole are some of the most interesting fights too, which made me happy.

All in all, it's worth your time. I loved running through this creepy world. One thing to note is that the first biome is probably the least intriguing, as it's essentially a decrepit Earth. Don't assume the game is just that, because it's not. There's more fantastical areas to come afterwards. The best areas are later in the game, in my opinion, so go give this one a shot!

Probably my favourite third-person shooter, the guns just feel great to use and character movement is so fluid. Love the setting/lore, love the enemy designs and world aestetics, love the awesome weapons and mods and the fact the mods even visually alter the weapons looks, love all the character build options. Crazy amount of replay value too, the main campaign will be different every time, even different area's, weapon/armour unlocks and bosses. There's also shorter form adventures to play and a rogue-like mode.

It won't be for everyone though, even on normal difficulty this is a hard game, especially some of the bosses (including the first one, took me over an hour to beat and I came close to giving up). I does click eventually though, a lot like the Dark Souls games the more you play the easier it becomes. I did play solo though, I'm pretty sure it would be more accessable in co-op.

One of the few games I've finished and then straight away started playing again and now I've pottered round solving puzzles and reading lore on my own, I guess it's time to try co-op.

I love this game. To those who say it's too short: you've seen about half the game at most. There are 40 bosses in total, if you include the DLC. 

It's procedural so each play-through includes different map layouts, special events, locations, bosses and enemies. Higher difficulties reveal special enemies and events you don't get at easier settings. 

If you don't fancy replaying the whole game - adventure mode is for you, which allows you to run through on area, with associated bosses and dungeons, meaning you can see most of the game barring certain inter-map bosses/encounters. Very roguelike, plenty to do way beyond a single story playthrough. There's at least one boss which spawns only in adventure mode. Excellent, bold move in the dev's part. After that there's also Survival Mode, where you start with very few items and play until you die ...

My main complaint: like many (RPG) games, it gets the difficulty curve wrong. It's at its hardest at the start, when you have no perks or special weapons and haven't quite worked out the skills. Dark Souls gets this right and the game remains a real challenge to the end. Remnant doesn't get super easy but it definitely gets easier. I started on "Normal" difficulty and it seemed like Normal difficulty would be enough... but by halfway through, with the weapons and mods I had, i realised it was getting too easy and had to restart - that being the only way to reset difficulty.

Secondly: the level of each area is based on your weapon/armour levels when you enter the area, with a heavy bias towards your single highest level item, so levelling one or two items quickly really works against you as other bits of gear lag behind. Tip: level everything just one level at a time (to keep them all at the same level). 

In general, it's better not to level gear unless you absolutely have to and want a bonus against the current area/boss, but you'll pay for it in the next when difficulty ramps up, since fighting higher level enemies makes them slightly harder and once you get to level 20, that's it. No more out-levelling the game by upgrading equipment - though new traits/skills will continue to make the game easier. 

I finished the main game + DLC with gear at level 16 (Hard difficulty) where in my first playthroughs I'd levelled one weapon to 20 in just by half way through. Not that this made the game excessively hard, barring a couple of bosses, but it does make the game experience inconsistent. Boss weapons which require special resources to upgrade only level to 10 and count double for difficulty purposes. So a level 8 boss weapon counts as if it's level 16 when calculating dificulty.

If you are playing in a party, playing coops, it uses the levels of the weapons carried by all players, so if someone has something super upgraded the others might find themselves having issues...even if that party member leaves, the area remains at the higher level once generated.

Players need to have all this explained to them so they definitely get it and there's no way they can miss it. Over and over. e.g. have a popup appear when they level a weapon which changes their effective level saying "Levelling this weapon to level 12 will increase your effective level from 11 to 12, which will increase the strength/difficulty of enemies in any new areas you enter, for your whole party. It will not affect enemies in locations you have already visited. Do you want to proceed?". At the moment I think the only place you can see your weapon level is on the opening character selection screen. 

The game takes no account of player level, traits/skills gained etc when setting difficulty, which seems odd. Even if it's just +1 level per 50,75 or even 100 trait points, some account should be taken.

Like Dark Souls, Remnant makes use of iframes - but never explicitly mentions or explains this and both games fall foul on this one. If you're new to the genre - iframes are grames of various animations during which a player usually will not take damage. Most obviously in rolls/dodges, so even if an enemy hits you and you're mid roll, you won't take damage. You're vulnerable at the start and finish of each roll, so it's not a get out of jail free card, and timing rolls is key, depending on the enemy attack, but it's an intended feature and not knowing about it is a hinderance. I don't know if Remnant does this but certainly in Dark Souls, the lighter your encumbrance, the further you roll and the less time you spend in the vulnerable 'getting up' and 'starting roll' animation phases ... but since Remnant does talk about armour encumbrance quite a bit, I assume that the heavier you armour the less effective your rolls, as a trade off...


There are weapons of different types, e.g. radiation, bleed, freeze, but apparently different enemies don't have different resistances. So, once I got my super bleed crossbow and a ring which transferred bleed damage to healing for me, I mostly stuck with it. TBH the crossbow as OPAF long before that, but the fact that I could, for example, cause bleed damage on a black hole seemed nonsense. Apparently this was a conscious decision by the devs who wanted all builds to work on all enemies, which to me seems like a really bad decision. It trivialises weapon choice, levelling, depth and reduces the longevity of the game. I mean, i had to grind up a fast firing weapon for the Ixillis boss fight one fight, as I didn't have one, and that's not too different to grinding up a weapon with say poison damage because you know it's particularly effective against certain enemies i'm having issues with.

Also: let me reset difficulty mid-way through a playthrough, instead of having to restart, so that all new areas generated are created with the new difficulty and I don't have to go back to the beginning. OK, so only credit me for having completed it at the lowest difficulty I set during any one playthrough but as long as you give me PLENTY of warning about this, that's fine. I am playing because I enjoy the gameplay. At most make me replay the area/zone I am in.

Also: make difficulty selection more apparent at the start of the game. There's a reason most games have it separate from the character designer: it's out of place and isn't part of the character creation process. Players don't expect to see it there, they're likely to miss it.

[H1]To-Buy or Not-to-Buy!?[/h1]

This is always the burning question I ask myself when a new prosperous game is released and like many gamers out there, I have a [i]very bad addiction[/i] for buying games and not playing them... So is this game worth a buy? Is it worth your money? Is it going to keep you captivated long enough before the next hit-title to come along and grab your attention?

The short answer - [b]Yes.[/b] It's completely and utterly worth your money.

If you want to know why, keep on reading.

[table]
    [tr]
        [th]Categories[/th]
        [th]Review[/th]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Graphics[/td]
        [td]The graphics are sublime; not all games are understandably about graphics and aesthetics, but let's face it, we're all guilty of enjoying a really well textured game and Remnant delivers quite nicely on providing you a well polished graphical game - you feel like you're playing a triple-AAA title and revving your graphic's card like a sports car by just looking at it. Graphics in a nutshell are superb.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Functionality[/td]
        [td]For a fairly high graphical game, it astounds me that the game it's self runs incredibly well. Not even big game developers [strike]*COUGH* like EA and Bethesda *COUGH*[/strike] can always get this right and release a final title that's full of bugs and feels like it's being powered by a potato. No, not in this game. For a small development team, they have done extremely well with providing what feels like an incredibly smooth experience and well made game. I haven't yet found a bug, noticed any lag or had to adjust my game's settings whatsoever. It runs like a dream, whilst keeping the high-paced combat flowing throughout. Very impressive and well made game.[/td]
    [/tr]
    [tr]
        [td]Combat[/td]
        [td]The combat mechanics are fairly simple, but it works! Each weapon has it's own perks and drawbacks, but this is the highlight of why it's so important to pick your two main weapons and then try sticking to them. You don't have a vast array of weapons to choose from; thus far I have in the region of perhaps fifteen to twenty weapons (including melee weapons) but by not having dozens and dozens of weapons to choose from, you choose what suits your play-style and then you upgrade and make altercations to that weapon as the game progresses. Overall, the combat is sleek and satisfying. Ever played Call of Duty and get that satisfying hit-marker come up when hitting an enemy? This game gives you a similar FPS buzz.

The only drawback I will mention with the combat mechanics, is that melee isn't great... But arguably, this game is focused around the FPS/Shooting aspect and therefore melee is only deemed a last-resort option of when  you run out of ammo.[/td]

Granted - as long as you reach a checkpoint (bright coloured stone to save your game) then you won't lose any story progression and even if you didn't save at a checkpoint, it's no major deal, the checkpoints are incredibly common within the world. You'll have one big firefight and then there will be a checkpoint shortly afterwards. So there is no penalty if you had to leave the game prior to completing a section of the game without saving. 

Everyone in the game also shares all the loot - meaning - if you find a new weapon, you'll all get that weapon! Same with materials and other items.

The only downside, is that the host's story will only be progressed. So if you fight a few bosses then go back to your own game, you would not have completed those bosses. You will keep all your loot you got (and any levels you have), but the story progression would not have carried over. This is because each world is unique and you may not have the same bosses in your game, compared to your friend's game. Which ideally gives the game a lot more re-playability. It's not a bad thing! and I say that as in. it takes inspiration from it. this game is hard, it kicked my ass a few times during the start but
it gives you that feel of not wanting to give up and theres alot more too it then what I expected.

(GAMEPLAY)
Its pretty straight foward. you got your melee, Primary and secondary weapon. mouse 1 uses your melee
while holding mouse 2 uses your gun. you always gotta aim with it, you cant spray and pray blindly into the field.
theres not a crap ton of guns to choose from but there is quite a variety. and some of them you unlock through hidden
areas or events. However there are mods that will give you a special ability inplanted into your gun and theres quite alot
of them to collect. they even change the appearance of your gun aswell when you equip them. starting off with pretty basic ones like a healing field or protection. to more Insane ones like spawning floating skulls to help you in combat.
You start off by choosing 3 classes and they all come with their own set of Traits.
Traits are basically your character perks and you'll discover more as you get further in the game. unlocking new stats and perks for your character like more health, more accuracy or more weapon damage. theres also alot of them aswell so you can build your character however you want.
While you explore the world you also come across these red crystals. these serve as your bonefires and theres two types of them. the big one is the bonefire that you can teleport around the world with. while the smaller ones are just there serving as checkpoints. everytime you visit one you get all your ammo refilled together with your health but all enemies around the area respawns aswell.

While exploring 90% of all the areas you come across are randomly generated. meaning that not everybody will have the same playthrough as the previous guy. you might discover things or come across events that others may not. and most of them rewards you with weapons, mods, armor or rings/necklace. This not only gives you alot of replayability but you can also farm for certain items in the game by using a feature called "Adventure mode" this one is based outside story mode.
same with Bosses some bosses show up in specific tilesets or they can show up when you least expect it. and to top it off theres tons of bosses to go through with alternate ones aswell.
Many of the enemies I came across weren't copy n paste version of other enemies I met before. they all were uniqe and acted in diffrent ways aginst you. but most of them will often rush you down and they are merciless too.

There is Coop too and its pretty straight foward compared to some other souls games were you gotta perform specific acts in order to summon your friend. You can choose if you want an open session or friend-only in the main menu and only 2 players can be with you however.
Once someone joins your session just go back to one of the crystals and the guy will pop out in no time. it can get pretty insane during combat when you for example are surrounded by sevural enemies and both you and your friends throw out your abilities at once.
Even with more players, the game can still give you a challange as most enemies can bring you down with 2-3 hits
so be on your guard while exploring together.

(STORY. I will keep this short)

Humanity is at the peek of the end as a mysterious ancient tree-like evil has taken over earth.
not only spreading it's roots across the lands but also spawning creatures to hunt down the humans.
you start off as a nobody whos traveling across the sea to find some sorta tower. you get washed away by
the storm and end up on an unknown location were you encounter "The root" after fighting your way through
you come across more humans and inside your base is were the "sanctuary" is at.
They fill you in about some person named Ford who seems like an important figure. so its up to you to go out there
and find him. but your task wont be easy as you will have alot of hell to go through. but dont worry as they will supply you with both armor and weapons. and also give you mods once in a while whenever you come back.
you'll discover more about the Root and unlock new secrets aswell.

Addicting replayability

Im Very Pleased with this game, I hope we'll be seeing more future content later as Im
hoping this game goes places and dosnt just stop when things are getting Good.
best of luck to Gunfire games as they have done an excellant job.

I don't write many reviews, but you shouldn't pass this game up. Here's some random tidbits.
Different bosses each playthrough, alternate kill methods resulting in different loot from them, different campaign events each time with satisfying and interesting rewards.
This is NOT a looter shooter, each piece of loot you receive is individually designed and specifically rewarded.
Progression is not done via skill tree or anything like that, if you play long enough you'll earn everything. You do decide on the order that you want to grow your character however. Each level requires the same amount of EXP to earn, whether it's your 2nd or your 600th, this results in very steady and regular/reliable progression.
Combat is satisfying and skillbased. Bosses will feel very difficult and unforgiving early on as you learn the mechanics. After your first or second boss and getting beaten down a bit, you'll feel much more confident moving forward however. Deaths tend to feel like your fault, rather than cheap mechanics.
I'll leave it there, don't spoil too much for yourself as you decide if it's for you or not, enjoy!

Great game. What seemed like an average adventure for 10-15 hours, eventually turnt into a place, where you want to stay for hundreds of hours. I can state that Remnant is old-fashioned in a good way. Like old movies from late 60th - early 70th. Today you may notice some evident flaws there, but they are still charming. Same here. While there are indeed some outdated gameplay mecanics or conventionalities - the game nevertheless has it's unique style and atmosphere, as well as some great gameplay features.

The first aspect that worth mentioning is an art style of monsters and locations. Definitely not something you can see everyday. How about Earth, infested with roots and overwhelmed by tree-like monsters, mutants and cultists? Or the world of eternal winter, inhabited by giant ratmen, armed with firearms? Or maybe a post-nuclear world, inhabited by mutated barbaric tribes, who use sorcery, explosives and nuclear weapons? 

Setting - great and unique as well. Not your typical post-apoc story where USA & USSR out of boredom made kabooom in 999th time. Here,  in order to survive, you have to visit other worlds and even dimensions, sometimes inhabited by creatures even more dangerous than the ones who destroyed the Earth. The game gives you tons of information about local setting via archaic computers, tape-recorders, letters and newspapers, but... you absolutely doesn't have to read any of this. And this is another great thing, because you can get more or less clear understanding of the situation without them.

Another great thing - soundtracks, which perfectly fit the amosphere. From gloomy and melancholic tunes when you are visiting dead streets of Earth or noisy swamps of Corsus (another world) - to dynamic and even epic compositions while you are fighting with local bosses.

One more strong aspect, and definitely the most important here - gameplay. Yes, not without flaws, but it has enough interesting mechanics to give you some great experience. And the best thing here is shooting. It's not just great, I'd even say that shooting here brings satisfaction. Each gun behaves differently. And their variety is also huge: from some self-made firearms and archaic guns from early and mid XX century - to some crazy alien guns, which can send enemies to another dimension, infest them with some bloodsucking bugs or even ressurect you on death.  

And this is not all. Each weapon can also be equiped with a special module, which can improve it's firepower or even give it some other useful effect. How about fire bullets which will burn enemies? Or maybe frost bursts, which can freeze even bosses? Maybe a healing aura? Or ability to spawn few minions? Most of these modules can be switched between most weapons (because some weapons have their unique modules which can't be changed) which gives you many options to create the best build for your playstyle.

And a word about builds. It's not just about weapons and modules. Each armor set also has it's unique bonuses: some of them give you the best protection at cost of mobility while others may give you huge boost to your overall damage or even  turn you into so-called vampire, who regenerates health by shooting enemies. And you also have a vast variety of rings and amulets to create your perfect build. Very often you can find something that seems rather useless. You may even think: "Who would even think to use this clearly [i]harmful[/i] garbage?" But then you may find some other ring, which can totally negate it's negative effect, or combine it with some set of armor so these negative effects just do not matter anymore.

There are also trait points you get after earning a certain amount of experience. You may invest them literally into everything: reload speed, weapons swap speed, running speed, firerate, protection, stamina, etc, etc. Thus, all this allows you to create your unique class. From the guy who can one-shot almost everyone to unkillable armored tank. From support guy, who heal and boost allies to summoner who uses lots of minions. All this creates greate environment for replayability.

While I love all abovementioned aspects, and especially the setting, I must admit that the story here kinda sucks. Tasks are vague, characters are bland, events are uninspiring... Talk with this aged boss woman, recover that ancient aged woman, find the main aged man. Get them all, lol, but instead of pokemons you are collecting old people here. Honestly, I was 10 times more interested in exploration of new locations with it's local "fauna" and artifacts, rather then searching for some elusive [strike]Joe[/strike] Ford.

One more thing I didn't like is... prologue/tutorial (you have to finish it before playing the actual game). It looks kinda... poor? And hardly represents main gameplay. It's short but I got bored very soon. If not my friend, who instantly dragged me to co-op, I'd probaly postpone the game for better times.

Now few words about real flaws. Unfortunately. There are few of them, but I see only one huge problem which can potentially burn your chair, make your eyes red and turn your hair white. And that's... network issues. The game uses peer-to-peer system. Thus, you have to pray for you Internet, or the Internet of the host. The situation where I was disconnected, or my teammates were disconnected are countless. No matter who is the host and where is he from - there is no guarantee that you or he will be disconnected.

And let me be clear about this situation. It is not that problematic if you play campaign or adventure with your friends or even random players. You can easily rejoin this game the moment later, because your mates can "reconnect" you from the nearest spawn stone. You won't even lose anything. But for survival mode network issues are fatal. Because there is no way to reconnect to the game in this mode. If a player gets disconnected, the game is ruined for him (it's kinda clear why) and potentially ruined for remained players, because they lose valuable asset forever. The moment you see your mate doing "moonwalk" on the head of the boss, in the air, or underground - you realise that few moments later he will get disconnected.

Another problem - bugs. And again, it is not a problem for campaign or adventure. But for survival mode they are critical. Boss fell underground - you can't kill boss, you can't leave the room, you can't move further, run is ruined. You decided to change armor piece - you... died. Lol, yeah, probably from heart attack. On island maps from Reism campaign, instead of beign incapacitated after you lose your health - you instantly die. And I mentioned only significant ones.

The last... hmm... really not that much a problem, but more like a claim. Steam backgrounds. I really rarely pay attention to stuff like this but... you have so many iconic and beautiful locations in your game and you put here those ugly NPCs instead? Why not cathedral? Alien nexuses with the black sun on background? Labyrinth? Ancient ruins among giant trees? What a waste...

Overall, even with all it's cons - highly recommend. Find yourself 2 more friends for better experience and you will get really unforgettable adventure. Of course game can be finished solo, but with friends it's faster, safer, more efficient and exciting.

Tbh, this game itself is just dope. After Dark Souls became a hit, heaps of soul-like games keep popping up. Some of them are extraordinary, some are just mimics with inferior quality.... But this one is special. 

I remember getting this game for free on Epic at some time last year, but I never play it because of Epic's lame multiplayer system (plus I ain't got no friend on that platform). So I bought this game during the Winter Sale on Steam (Top 10 anime betrayal, XD). When I played it on singleplayer mode, I felt like I was playing a soul-like Borderlands: mobs are tough but not as troublesome as those Dark Souls monsters, map is big with many secret spots, and u can collect materials for upgrading and even rare gears. What's more, the modeling of characters are good, sometimes there are glitches but most of the time are a-okay. Remarkably, the weapons gained via purchasing or boss fights are flashy: Some are with special effects, some are just cool as heck, and when u buy the dlcs, there will be more fancy weapons or gears, :).

When you go for multiplayer mode, things are getting quite interesting. Three dudes can co-op in a good way, fighting off countless foes, or just get shit-faced and teabag each other. The most impressive fight I had with friends was the boss fight with the Ravager, a wolf-like colossal beast. In order to lure him out, players should ring the bells in order in front of his little cave, or you can just poke his cocky nose with your sword. At first, we didn't really know the order, so we kinda fussed and shit happened, someone accidentally hit the wolf's face, and we immediately entered the boss fight, unprepared and fked up. Anyway, the PvE mode is just pure fun. Besides, there are survival mode and adventure mode available for players, which are also pretty intriguing with some special quests. 

One thing I felt bad about is the story. No need for spoiler text here cuz all I remember is me being asked to save this save that, meeting a bunch of different people and going to many weird places, and the story just ended. I thought it would be more after the final boss fight but it didn't. So all I could recall were some tough boss fights and me roaming around a vast region with countless mobs. So, to me, it's quite hard to gather those fragmented info because I am a lazy guy who always skip reading texts. Also, in order to understand the story well, I need to play its prequel, which is just mediocre compared to this one.

Anyway, it is a pretty wholesome game, pretty much meet my needs during Christmas. If you are a big DS fan and wanna try something new, give this game a shot!

On sale I'd say it's worth it. I have mixed feelings about the game. It has many bosses, it has a decent story (just an opinion), and is has a decently sized world. 

It took me 12 hours on my first playthrough to finish the game. 

So I decided to give adventure mode a swing at higher difficulties... the thing is that the difficulty scaling just makes getting hit more punishing and it makes the bosses bullet sponges, or any enemy for that matter on apocalypse. I don't consider this to be "difficult", I consider it to be a time waste. It is in the same boat as jump scares being categorized as "horror".

Does that mean that the game is no fun? Absolutely not. It just would've been a lot more fulfilling if a higher difficulty meant that the bosses would get actually more difficult. For example new mechanics, attacks etc. Up until the final boss they are all pretty much brain dead. 

I will keep playing it for a bit more, because I want to see how broken my build can become, but playing on higher difficulties holds no merit for me. It is literally doing the same tactics, but instead of 5 minutes it takes 35-40 minutes on apocalypse. Higher difficulties also give the same rewards, other than XP. I understand that they don't want to force people to play higher difficulty game modes, but they could've made it more... difficult. Bullet sponges is not the way to go, but at the end of the day, that is just my opinion. I bet plenty of people reading this are a lot less picky than I am and for them it can be a very enjoyable experience.

I tried this game coop with my brother. It strikes quite a nice balance between challenging and relaxing. Some of the bosses are extremely surprising - at first blush, they are tanky and hit hard and you have no idea how shooting for longer or dodging 99% instead of 95% of their attacks is interesting -  as you understand what mechanics you could use to gain leverage over them, some of them become downright fascinating; intrigues of game design.

Some of the fights you can tell are scaled for three people, and doing them with two is difficult but rewarding.

I played the last 2/3rds and the expansions via online coop with strangers and realized this game is meant to be played exactly like Diablo 2. You join games and quest with randos, but you also often will help them with a quest that you do not have and vice versa. This leads you to discover NPCs and areas in a region (which will be located differently in your game-world, each person's being randomly generate - some NPCs or areas may even be absent in exchange for another) which you may not have found yourself, and you establish some piecemeal comprehensions of future quests which you may endeavor. 

The feeling, later on, of working in parties and sometimes knowing (without any language - there is no viable media for written lingual communications implemented in the game) what quests others are on, sometimes realizing that they know what quests you are on (and how they should be done, when they step into a guest leadership mode and rush you along the key events) is wonderful. 

When the piecemeal comprehensions come together finally - you spend an hour or two doing a quest, and you see a few familiar items or NPCs or locations, and suddenly you understand what other events were related to those items or NPCs - the sense of satisfaction is very strong. When it begins to happen more frequently, as you have several pieces of several puzzles in your knowledge - It completely changes your opinion on what the game you are playing *is*. You change from a vacationer & a follower into a custodian & a leader as you hit the three objectives you now know were related. You understand the NPC dialogues and cutscenes that you have already seen as they slot into your newly enlightened perspective. 

Because of how this works, it is not for those who demand to know everything up front. This is a lot like Diablo 2 - you want to do boss runs for loot, you want to run with groups for safety - and in so doing, you accidentally discover foundational narrative perspectives & significant questlines. 

There is also not so much going on that you are not given the opportunity for insight; the size of this game is a perfect one for the Diablo 2-style, experience-minutiae-as-a-follower-first, emergent comprehension of the broadest picture. thirty or forty hours of play, mostly playing coop in regions you are in (and thus often helping people a little ahead in one of your quest lines), with some play with significantly higher level people in unknown regions and some showing people below you how to proceed, results in a total experience which is magical. You have insight into all possible worlds - being RNG, you need to play coop to understand this - and understand leading & following in each region and along each questline.

It is hard to say what the best way to play this is. It's good private co-op with a personal friend, wherein the outstanding part is how fun a shooter it is and how good some boss fights are, but I recommend it foremost as a solo online experience akin to Diablo 2, with a balance around 3:1 guest-host world experience.

Remnant: From the Ashes is a souls-like looter shooter, taking place in an alternate version of Earth. After creating your character in the admittedly barebones character creator, you set out on a quest to stop the Root, a mysterious invading force that hunts down humanity. What follows is an adventure across worlds, taking you to interesting places, introducing you to new characters, and providing tons of new enemies to battle. The game is randomly generated, meaning no two characters have the same exact experience. Keep in mind though, that doesn't mean the world is cobbled together by an algorithm; rather, the game simply orientates well crafted areas differently each time, throwing different bosses and enemies in.

The gameplay was MADE for me. As someone who's a big fan of souls-like combat, and also likes shooters that don't require you use cover, this was so much fun to play. One character I played was a sniper themed character that focused on long rifles and crits, and another(my favourite) was a shotgunnier that focused on maneuvering and dealing damage close up. Although your starting class does have an effect on future gameplay, the game is still pretty flexible in terms of the gear you can use. On the second character for example, there were times where I would switch to a sniper rifle in areas full of ranged opponents, and it would work just fine with my skills.

Unlike most souls-like games, you can actually choose the difficulty. I mention this because playing on harder difficulty provides "glowing shards", a currency that allows you to buy skins for the outfits. These unlocks are account wide, which is honestly just cool. It shows the effort you put into beating difficult bosses, and is earned purely through gameplay.

One interesting aspect are the weapon mods. These offer special abilities, such as powerful attacks, buffs, or even summons, to aid you in combat. Some weapons come with a mod, whereas others allow you to switch them out with mods you've collected. I had fun mixing and matching these abilities. As for permanent stat bonuses, you get those from Traits. I like the idea that you collect traits as the game goes on, but usually these traits require a lot of investment to be useful. It would just be nice if you could reconfigure your traits throughout the game, so that you can make use of one you find later in the game.

My biggest criticism has to do with the balancing. You can beat this game solo, and throughout 80% of the game I didn't notice any issues, but there was the occasional boss that was clearly balanced for multiple people, and these were frustrating to get through. These bosses weren't even particularly difficult, most of the time it was simply because I would get overwhelmed by a ridiculous amount of adds. There was only one  playthrough where I managed to beat a particularly egregious boss, and it was one where I managed to find two summon mods to help balance the fight(keep in mind, the game is randomly generated. Aside from the dog one which you unlock for all characters, finding the other was luck).

As for the story, it's interesting but not fun to discover. A good portion of it is told through journals that are several pages long and emails on computer terminals. Other times, a disinterested NPC will provide a history lesson that's boring to listen to. There's also quite a few plotpoints that are strangely dropped or don't have the affect they should. Like, on one planet you're introduced to a rebellion, but that ends up going nowhere. And on a couple planets, despite becoming allies with the local rulers, the inhabitants still attack you on sight. Some important actions will get a handfull of characters to mention the impact, but most of the time the NPC's act like nothing's changed. As far as game stories goes, it's got some interesting moments but overall it's not the best.

Although it has some flaws, Remnant is still extremely fun, offering a shooter based souls-like experience I most likely will find myself return to. I haven't got the DLC yet, but I definitely plan on doing so in the future.

[h1]Third person looter shooter with souls-like RPG mechanics and procedural generation.[/h1]

[i]Dark souls with guns!¡!¡![/i] Well, kinda.
The fact that this games borrows heavily from the [i]Soulsborne formula[/i] is immediately evident: exploration segments marked by checkpoints which allow you to teleport, stamina management, fog gates, boss encounters which require multiple attempts (although dying in this game doesn't result in loss of currency/XP), musical cues underlining particular events and the fact that gear takes precedence over stats/skills, so you can basically pick a class at the beginning of the game and may end up with a completely different character build type, if you so desire.
The way in-game currency, XP and skill points are handled in this game strays from the DS path in favor of a more traditional RPG system.
An interesting addition to the formula is that character skills (or [i]traits[/i]) are unlocked upon completion of hidden objectives.

The game world is not seamless: main world hubs connect smaller quest areas and the whole world structure (including [b]which[/b] quest areas will be available) is procedurally generated at the beginning of the campaign. This means you [b]won't[/b] be able to complete every side quest, face every boss and get every piece of gear during a single playthrough. The addition of [i]Adventure Mode[/i] now allows players to generate a separate portion of the campaign in order to get particular side quests or items, without having to reroll the main campaign and start from scratch.


The known downside of procedural generation is the generic feel and repetitiveness of level design and this game is no exception: from time to time I almost feel like I'm playing an incredibly underpopulated lag-free MMO, but the gameplay itself is enough to keep me entertained and also overlook the lack of lore depth and the early-2000s-grade facial animations of the few NPCs you encounter.

Coop remedies to some degree to the "emptiness" of the game world and is personally preferable to solo sessions, if somewhat easier. However, since cheaters can negatively affect your game and cause your character to be soft banned, I strongly advise against playing with random people and [i]only host/join game session with trusted friends[/i] and even then I suggest to regularly make a back up copy of your game save, in case you're as unlucky as me to incur in the annoying situation I described in [url=https://steamcommunity.com/app/617290/discussions/0/1735506178506484442/][u]this thread[/u][/url].

The game looks and performs as well as expected from a semi-indie Unreal Engine 4 project, although unfortunately my i7-6700K 4GHz and GTX 1070 don't manage to keep stable 60 fps on 1080p ultra settings, with occasional frame drops in the 40s when scoping or when the screen is particularly busy.
Keyboard and mouse controls are responsive and work without having to fiddle with smoothing, negative acceleration et similia; I can't provide any feedback on gamepad since I rarely use it, nor do I plan to.

All things considered, I feel the game is slightly overpriced and I'd recommend to wait for a sale, like I did (27,99€ a few months from release was fair).

[b]The game technically:[/b] [i]Remnant: From The Ashes[/i] is less about "getting good" (old jargon from the Souls series), and much more about "getting good together". The game itself is a coop game, not exclusively but almost. Even though playing single-player is an option, all of its mechanics revolve around cooperative work on defeating bosses/monsters over 8 levels/worlds (including DLCs). Everything seems to have been developed for this purpose. The gameplay, speaking about camera positioning, resembles much more [i]Resident Evil 4[/i] than the [i]From Software[/i] games (series the devs try to mimetize), even the Level Design and positioning of enemies, making the need of "rotation" around the map to avoid a large amount of them ganking you, however, instead of just shooting at monsters as in RE4, is established here a more paced/stamina consuming style of play, using the "dodge" to avoid enemy attacks (if you get hitted, it can destroy a large part of your HP) and privileging making critical hits. It is possible to choose classes and weapons which, of course, changes the style of play, but not the difficulty, a fact that makes the coop indispensable. But we have very poor amount of choices of items, what is disappointing. The game tries to differentiate itself in the Souls Like market by bringing the coop and mainly guns (Dark Souls with guns they say!). Graphically/aesthetically Remnant is irregular, the scenarios are sometimes very beautiful, but while distant of the sight, close by, characters, enemies and scenarios are poor, presenting jagged edges, shadows with poorly planned directions and expressionless characters with little characterization and detail. The textures are lazy and blurry in some areas and at procedurally generated maps (Adventure and Survival modes) show their flaws with a lot of CTRL + C and CTRL + V and not enough asset variety. The music is much more of a background than something with significant attention or something you want to listen, most of the time you not even notice it. The sound design/sound effects is enough to not disturb: the enemies scream, the weapons make [i]pew-pew[/i], as well as explosions, steps, clothes etc, the voice-acting is bad with very little variation, maybe only a phrase for a character/enemy, and some contextual responses and lines, but eventually they are repeated extensively throughout the game. No 3D sound, which is sometimes is impossible to know where an attack comes from except with the UI indicators. Remnant is not heavy on hardware/system for modern PCs, but it is unstable, having quite a few frame drops (-10 FPS~) in some areas. The bugs/glitches hardly break the gameplay completely, but are present all the time, with enemies appearing and disappearing, very bad choices of collision spaces, with your character getting hooked by small places/objects and damage being received outside the positioning area of ​​the graphic model. The difficulty is well balanced, but it lacks on being regular, with a common boss or enemy not following the difficulty pattern of the area/world, buuuut I admit that can be fun more than necessarily frustrating due to the surprise effect. The RNG/procedural/roguelike mechanic is not well planned to make the maps refresh enough, making it still tiring and visually repetitive for completionist players. The DLCs are not long enough or good enough to take much of this review, it could be in the base game too, but do not costs much and completes the game well, and gives a satisfying content.

I've played the game for a bit over 50 hours now and to say I'm addicted to it would be an understatement. This game has 4 difficulties (excluding "Hardcore" which deletes your character upon death) 

- Normal: A casual yet still fairly challenging (if you play solo) playthrough. You can enjoy the story easier and there is a LOT to read (so I kinda recommend playing solo for the story) and immerse yourself in.

- Hard: A slightly more difficult but still manageable mode, not over the top but provides a fair and balanced difficulty increase. Still easy for squads of 3 but you'll probably still die a few times anyways.

- Nightmare: You guessed it, it's a nightmare. The game for some reason decided to make the difference between Normal/Hard and Nightmare/Apocalypse literally massive. Enemies have way more health and some mobs can 2 shot you. Yeah, it's hard. However if you are playing with a trio and have some experience I HIGHLY recommend trying this difficulty out, it's a lot of fun (personally) for me and my friends to experience an actual challenge together. I will say, however; that for some this difficulty may prove to be too much.

- Apocalypse: You will die. Many times. Will you persevere or beg for mercy? That, my friend; is up to you. This difficulty will break you down, you may even rage. But if it isn't satisfying to kill a boss on this difficulty I don't know what is. Truly this is a difficulty level for true gamers.

I should also add that aside from the main story and difficulty there is also Survival Mode which has no effect on the main campaign *(apart from unlocking rewards by killing a number of bosses in one run)* and Adventure Mode which doesn't rewrite your main campaign but allows you to farm resources and retry an area to get different bosses freely. I will also add that you CAN in fact reroll your campaign at any time you so desire, allowing you to change the difficulty and everything. 

Benefits to each game mode.

Main Campaign - Story Progression, Loot, Unlocks
Adventure Mode - Loot, Unlocks
Survival: Unlocks

Tips

- I recommend playing Single Player on Normal difficulty, you can change difficulty at any time anyways to make the game more challenging if you so desire by rerolling campaign or doing a quick Adventure Mode instance. 

- I recommend playing Survival Mode with 3 players (preferably friends and with a stable connection) as playing it solo is really difficult and time consuming, not to mention if you end up getting knocked down it's GG.

- I recommend not restarting main campaign if you want to get a different boss weapon/items because you can just use the Adventure Mode to farm them, it's all luck based regardless.

- Your equipment level will determine your in-game difficulty, meaning if your friend starts a new character and you are on a character with level 20 gear, your friend will be getting absolutely destroyed by the easiest mobs in the game because his equipment won't be up to standard. Remnant: From the Ashes is one of the surprise hits for me in 2019. I knew I was going to like it based on the preview videos and streams, but I didn't expect it to be as good as it is.

[h1][b]General gameplay[/b][/h1]
At it's core Remnant is a shooter with some melee combat elements, which might be familiar if you have played Dark Souls.
It can be played completely solo, or up to 3 players drop-in/drop-out co-op.
The controls are very tight and responsive as you would expect from a game like this, and the shooting feels very satisfying.
The game features procedual map generation, so each time you re-roll the world, or join other player's campaign it will fee a little bit different.

[h1][b]Character progression[/b][/h1]
When it comes to character progression Remnant is a little bit different from other games. 
Each time you level up you gain a trait point, which can be spent on already available passive skills: increase base HP, more stamina, etc. However as you traverse the world you discover new skills by completing specific objectives (EG: complete quest, kill boss etc)  or meeting certain conditions (EG: revive teammates X times, getting downed X times etc)
Besides killing enemies and completing quests, Trait points can be earned by finding Tomes of Knowledge. These items are scattered around the world and will automatically grant you 1 point. This makes exploration all the more worthwhile.


[h1][b]Combat mechanics[/b][/h1]
Remnant's combat system is mixture of close and long range combat.
The melee combat is a combination of light and heavy attacks, while your dodging (tied to Stamina) is affected by your armor weight.
Yes, you can achieve the infamous fat roll from Dark Souls.😉

The guns consist of the usual categories, such as handguns, revolvers, shotguns, SMGs, but energy based weapons also make an appearance in the late game. 
One of the key features of the game are the weapon mods, that you can attach and unattach to any gun you like. 
These mods grant you powerful skills and can significantly change how you play the game: 
You like to fire incendiary bullets? There's a mod for that.
Launching grenades from a handgun? Sure thing. 
Boss has a huge HP pool and always ducks into cover? Launch a swarm on him that periodically drains his HP!
Or you just need to cast a healing aura for the team? Again, there's a mod for that.

[h1][b]The shooting gallery: Bestiary and Bosses[/b][/h1]
But what do good combat mechanics mean if there's no worthy foe to shoot at? Well worry not, in the 4 worlds of Remnant, all with distinct biomes, you will have plenty of creatures to unleash hell upon. 
From teleporting archers to pesky summoners and berzerkering brutes you will find everything.
Each of them have nice movesets and will provide a challenge in groups, as their skills complement each other well.

And then of course there's the bosses, the main attraction of the game.
There are more than 20 of them, and since the game has procedual generation, you might not encounter some of them in your playthrough, but run into different ones when joining another player's world.
When it comes to bosses there are world bosses, that are mandatory for story progression and there are optional bosses that can be found in dungeons.
Each of them can come in "vanilla form" or with modifiers (higher HP, increased damage etc) to provide some extra challenge.
They are tough and they will often make you rethink your strategy and loadout. 
Luckily though due to the nature of the weapon mods you can easily adapt your playstyle on the go. 
It's important to mention that all bosses have respawning adds, so if you are easily frustrated then this game is might not be for you.
Defeating a boss will grant you a fix reward, so you don't need to worry about having to farm them over and over for an item that you need.

[h1][b]Not without an issue[/b][/h1]
Unfortunately there's no such thing as a perfect game, and Remnant is no exception.
In my 20 hour playtime I experienced 3 crashes only, however 2 of those were triggered by interacting lore items in my friend's world, so that number could have been higher.
In certain areas you can clip through the floor and enemies can get stuck inside walls. These bugs are not frequent, but they are certainly there.

Procedual map generation is one of the game's selling point, but at the same time it's one of its weaknesses as well. Due to the system, no location really stands out and sometimes the same tiles (same location, same item arrangement) are very close to each other.


[h1][b]Summary[/b][/h1]
Despite some of it's issues, Remnant is a very enjoyable game with high replay value and plenty of content to keep you busy.
And after the stinkers AAA publishers dropped this year (I'm looking at you Bethesda), this game is a breath of fresh air, especially for this price.

Highly recommended!

Remnant: From the Ashes is a third-person action shooter built on procedural world layouts and high difficulty. The player faces an invasion of corrupt creatures called the Root and travels between realms to stop the spread. The story is minimal and acts mainly as context for combat progression and exploration.

Core gameplay blends ranged and melee attacks. Weapons have mod slots that grant abilities like summoning allies or firing elemental bursts. Positioning matters because enemies rush and flank frequently. Dodge rolls carry invincibility frames and define survival at higher difficulties.

Progression centers on gear upgrades and traits. Traits grant passive bonuses that improve damage, stamina, survivability, or resource gain. Many are unlocked by completing hidden events. This rewards curiosity and encourages multiple runs. Armor sets add bonuses that support focused playstyles.

World design is semi-random. Each campaign generates different dungeons, bosses, and quests. This variability increases replay value but can gate specific items behind new runs. Some encounters maintain high difficulty spikes that require gear checks and team coordination.

Enemy variety changes by region. Factions have distinct attack patterns and elite units. Boss fights often spawn additional mobs, forcing constant movement. Weapon mods and elemental builds help control crowds and break resistances. Team play amplifies these strengths.

Visual presentation uses overgrown urban ruins, alien deserts, and corrupted forests. Sound design telegraphs heavy attacks with clear audio cues. Performance is stable, though some boss arenas feel cramped. Music underscores tension with rhythmic percussion.

Remnant: From the Ashes targets players who enjoy challenging combat loops, loot progression, and replay variability. Solo play is viable, but co-op improves pacing and survivability. Fans of souls-influenced shooters will find satisfying depth and long-term build experimentation.

[h1]One of my favorite games but I can't recommend it for two reasons.[/h1]

1)  It actively tries to deceive and manipulate the players via a false sense of progression.

2)  It's autosave-only which means that you can easily lose everything unless you manually back up your files outside of the game (It happened to a friend I was playing with.)

[h1]Short:[/h1]

Remnant From the Ashes is literally my favorite game from the point of view of its ground controls and combat. If STO had ground combat like Remnant, it would be (in my opinion) the greatest game to be made so far (take note of that ARC games.)

Unfortunately, this game is autosave-only which means that if your autosave gets corrupted, you will lose everything unless you have backed up your saves manually by locating them and copying them to a different folder. (Instructions on how to do that are at the bottom of the review.)

The integrity of this game is also compromised by a counter-intuitive, treadmill-like, level-scaling system so broken that upgrading your weapons makes you weaker relative to the enemies. Upgrading actually makes you weaker... sad. Even worse, it sometimes is necessary because while the enemies will scale up, they won't scale down so if you don't upgrade, you will be badly under-leveled.

The boss battles can also feel cheap and frustrating. Most bosses simply spawn ads faster than a gremlin in a water fountain and some of them are much harder to defeat in coop (I played most of the game in coop but needed to do two boss battles alone in order to advance.)

[h1]Long:[/h1]

Deeply ambivalent about this game...

[h1]The good:[/h1]

Movement and general combat system are second to none.

The music is very nice.

The world is is reminscent of the one C.S. Lewis created for The Magician's Nephew. It's very interesting and full of possibilities.

The combat CAN be a nice blend of shooting, dodging and hack & slash... at least until the bosses start spamming adds and healing themselves.

Joining other people's games just works (you join games rather than sending invites but you can still easily play with your friends by having the host set the game to friends only and then having the other players simply use the option to join a friend's game.)

[h1]The bad:[/h1]

Boss battles can be tedious and very unfair since the bosses are just cheap having lots of adds, a ridiculous number of hitpoints (this can make you hate your weapons) and the ability to dodge, teleport and kill you in a hit or two ESPECIALLY when you have to slow down to use a healing potion. 

I actually liked the design and rhythm of some of the bosses so it really is sad that they decided to turn so many of them into rabbit lords that just spawn minions like a gremlin in a water fountain. The add spamming actually makes the bosses feel less unique since regardless of how the bosses work, every boss battle basically turns into fight the adds and try to get in a few shots to chip away at the boss while avoiding artillery strikes and poison which the cheap boss will keep spamming at you along with the infinite minion spawns. 

The leveling system is a counter-intuitive treadmill. The bosses and enemies level up to always be one higher than your most powerful piece of gear with the result that rather than feeling stronger as you level up your gear, you often end up feeling weaker instead. To quote the devs:

"So, if you have a +5 gun (so level 6 behind the scenes), a +3 secondary gun, a +2 sword, and +1 armor (all 3 slots) your weighted afterage is about level 5. Now, each NEW area you go into will be 5+1 (your level +1, so 6). Your level 6 gun will be doing work, and your armor will be below-par for enemies in that level 6 zone."

In other words, the game's "scaling" treadmill not only ensures that you do not really get stronger but also you can't even choose to prioritize one class of item since all the enemies will be "scaled" to your best item hence you must level everything you plan to use to the same level without prioritizing anything. This means that you will either play a mediocre character with no particular talents or a weak character with no particular talents. 

The weapons are underwhelming precisely because of the bullet-sponge bosses and the treadmill leveling system. I can't appreciate a weapon which can't even kill low level trash without multiple hits no matter how many times I upgrade it and when I see the weapon I upgraded so many times being virtually useless against a boss, I frankly stop valuing the weapon. The weapon then ceases to exist in my mind as a weapon and simply becomes a contrived mechanic to draw out the battles on the assumption that if a well-organized team of people can kill a boss quickly, then the game is somehow ruined since it says in the complete hack's guide to game development that boss battles should always take at least fifteen minutes.

I would like to recommend the game but I must do so with a warning. To get a good experience out of this, you need to metagame to keep your gear level down and avoid re-rolling. Even then, you will still get in trouble in endgame because the max level for the enemies is higher than the max level for your gear and abilities. This is partially compansated for by the fact that you can get passive skill bonuses but even if you do everything right, you will finish the game about as strong relative to the average enemies as you started out.

An additional wrinkle is the fact that weapons with built-in mods (boss weapons) are actually twice the level they say they are so you need to upgrade them to exactly half the level of your other gear.

Honestly this game probably would have been better without any RPG-leveling at all. A level up system that doesn't actually allow you to bceome stronger is worse than no level-up system at all.

Jim Sterling, who rarely meets a Soulslike game he doesn't like, doesn't recommend this and given that he found the constant feeling of getting stronger in Dark Souls, I think it's possible that he might have actually liked the game if it weren't for the level-scaling.

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3N3PgYxf6JM

To sum up, this game has great combat and an interesting world but it's design is somewhat undermined by a leveling scaling system designed to prevent you from actually getting stronger and a save system that requires working outside the game to back up your files.

Remnant is a looter-shooter with great feeling guns, great boss fights, inspiring world design and art direction, gorgeous music, intriguing lore, and good co-op potential. Remnant is not a full-priced title and it's difficult not to treat it like one, I say that as a good thing. Remnant presents itself so well and has so many good things going for it that my gripes at the title's shortcomings are not because I think the game is bad, but because it's good and I want it to be BETTER.

That being said, the game isn't perfect. The level-up system is a little jank (if you don't pick occultist as your class and max that class trait out immediately EVERY GIRL will laugh at you), the narrative disappears after a few hours and you're left with beautiful worlds with no real characters to compliment them, and an abhorrent lack of variety in the loot spewing from every hole you've shot into the enemy leave some glaring flaws on what is very obviously a wonderful gem of a game.

If all of that sounds enticing, or bearable, and you're down to spend $40 to feed a team of hungry hungry video game devs, then get the heck over here and shoot some trees with us. The devs are extremely diligent about listening to player feedback and are constantly responding to posts on their Reddit (or so I hear; there's no photographic evidence I have ever intentionally visited a sub-reddit of any caliber) and have made many a promise on more good content to come. For the rest of gamers out there that find most of what I posted either putrid, confusing, pretentious or a frothing mix of all three, you might not find much to sate your voracious and gluttonous appetite here. My advice: message your closest hipster and convince him to gift you a copy so he can finally play with someone, but be prepared for him to force-feed you the story.

Wow! What a pleasant and unexpected surprise. I had my eye on this game for a little while now, being drawn in by the world and art style. I almost jumped in solo, but found a friend to play through with.

From the top, many people call it a third person shooter spin on Dark Souls, and that's about as close to the truth as you can get with a simple explanation. I could already gush a long time about this game, but I'll just break down a few of my favorite points, as well as some points that I'm mixed on. I'll try to be spoiler-lite for those who like lore and world in their games.

[h1]LIKED:[/h1]
- [b]COMBAT:[/b] I know this is very general, but the moment to moment combat and gameplay feels very strong. My friend and I started at Normal difficulty, and at first we were worried it was going to be too easy - the first "areas" felt incredibly unthreatening. While I'm sure we could have still bumped up the difficulty, Normal difficulty still ramped up to give us a bit of a challenge in the worlds and especially bosses while not being [i]too[/i] sweaty. Keep in mind the i-frames for your dodges are [i]very[/i] forgiving so use your dodges as much as you can. If you want more of a challenge, definitely either play solo or bump up the difficulty once or twice as a group. There ended up being a lot more enemy variety than I expected, the boss fights are mostly very unique and fun, and it just feels good to play. WARNING: Try to figure out what difficulty you want to stick with early on in the game, because I believe you have to re-roll your entire campaign if you want to adjust the difficulty, unfortunately.
- [b]GEAR:[/b] Let's be clear, this isn't a LOOTER SHOOTER. Although the combat loop might play closer to an ARPG, there isn't loot raining from enemies. Loot is curated well by the developers, mainly unlocked from hidden areas, vendors, or drops from bosses, and the worlds themselves are full of basically crafting materials that help you to upgrade your gear. The armors all have different set bonuses, encouraging you to either mix and match for a lot of different passives, or double down on a particular set if you really like a set bonus for your build. Weapons, accessories, and "mods" (get to that in a second) are all easily swappable and encourage build experimentation.
"Mods" are basically your abilities, and they are attached directly to your weapons for the most part. So you're only going to probably have at max a few abilities equipped at a time, but again, since they exist as "mods" that can attach to items, they are easily swappable. (There are certain unique mods that are tied to specific weapons/items that cannot be swapped) There are some really really cool abilities attached to different mods, items, weapons, and armors that can create very unique builds depending on your playstyle.
- [b]REPLAYABILITY/CHOICE:[/b] We tried to mainly play through this game blind, but every now and then we would look something up on the wiki if we were confused, and there are a LOT of things in this game that encourage you to replay. For instance, there are entire bosses that will randomly spawn in a playthrough, and in other playthroughs they won't spawn at all. This also happens with random events and side quests. Even with certain bosses, depending on HOW you approach them or defeat them can completely change the encounter or the loot at the end of the fight - you can even outright avoid or cause boss fights, depending on your choices.
However, some people might already be thinking "aw man, does that mean if I find out about an item/quest/choice that I missed or should have done differently way after the fact, I have to either start the game over completely or wait until my next playthrough?" Thankfully, the devs thought of this, as well. Without going into too much detail, you can basically "re-roll" or "re-instance" certain areas specifically for this sort of thing, without affecting the main campaign progress of that character. Awesome.
- [b]LOOOOOORE:[/b] You can just blaze through this game and skip the story if you're not into that sort of thing. A ton of lore is kept in journals, computer terminals, and other things lying around the world. NPCs who have a ton of lore for you even give you a way to skip their dialogue or tell them you're not interested.
However, if you ARE interested, there is a LOT of lore for you to dig into! My friend and I took it slow, read lore bits everywhere we could find them, exhausted NPC dialogue options, and really really enjoyed getting pulled into the world. If you're a fan of eldritch/cosmic horror type stuff like me, you'll probably like this.
- [b]ROGUELITE MODE:[/b] My friend and I pretty much waited for each other to come online before continuing our story progress, but during a lunch break one day I [i]really[/i] had the itch to play more without messing up our co-op progress. That's when I saw the Survival mode. At some point the devs updated the game with a Roguelite mode - start from scratch at a hub world, enter dungeon, fight boss, return to hub world for more upgrades, rinse repeat. It's honestly a lot of fun, and even though you don't carry any of that loot out of the mode, you [i]can[/i] unlock a specific currency that can be used to buy transmog items in the main game. Pretty cool, imo, and yet more awesome replayability.

[h1]MIXED:[/h1]
- [b]MELEE:[/b] With the inspiration this game took from Soulsborne games, I tried to be more melee focused at the beginning of the game. I was actually thinking ammo would run out a lot faster and be a lot more scarce (it might be at higher difficulties), but the melee in this game doesn't feel... great. It's not bad! But at least on Normal difficulty, we found ourselves mostly resorting to ranged stuff and only using melee when I was in a bad spot or needed to push through a couple enemies to get more ammo. Some melee weapons feel better than others, though, so it's possible it just didn't click with me. Someone who possibly focuses on a melee focused build might enjoy it better, but I do hope they work on the overall feel of melee combat for the sequel. (Note: After playing the game more, I feel a bit more positive on this aspect, but I still do hope they improve on melee in the sequel.)

[h1]DISLIKED:[/h1]
- [b]CO-OP STORY PROGRESSION:[/b] This is not an issue that affected me personally, but I wanted to mention it since I found out about it. Co-op progression seems to only be tied to the HOST of that session. Yes, connected friends will unlock items and character progression that will remain persistent, but if they return to their own world, none of that story progress will count. My friend and I only played when we were both online so this wasn't an issue for us, but it's something to keep in mind.

Will update this review once I'm done with the main campaign and maybe dabble with DLC, but all in all this game was a wonderful surprise and I'm greatly enjoying it. I honestly think it's probably worth it at full price. If it's on sale and you're on the fence, I highly recommend it even more.
